description: A user signs up, logs back in, and reads their own data with the session they were handed. The same spec then drives ADR 0008 across the seam: a licence key is a giftable bearer claim that unlocks exactly one active account. The lane's Gumroad stub keys the sale on the licence key, so a second signup presenting the same key under another email is refused with the generic invalid_license and never learns the key was valid; deleting the first account through DELETE /users/me erases the binding (the receipt names licensebinding) and one new account then redeems the same key, inheriting access and nothing else; a third attempt is refused again. Backend suites prove the atomicity and the byte-identical refusals with an in-process client; this is the one place the production client, the Postgres UNIQUE constraint on gumroad_sale_id and the deletion cascade are exercised together. One journey rather than two because the ledger lets a spec cover exactly one journey.

A user who cannot log in asks for a reset from ForgotPasswordScreen, reads the email that arrives, follows the https link a browser can actually open, sets a new password on ResetPasswordScreen, and logs in with it; the "this wasn't me" arm cancels the token instead. This is the journey the outage came through: reset mail went to a production log for one reason and carried nothing but an adepthood:// deep link for another, and the endpoint answered 202 through both while every backend suite stayed green. The spec reads the plaintext token out of the rendered body and out of nowhere else, anchored on the https origin APP_BASE_URL configured, so a body that offered only the deep link fails it. The lane reaches that body by booting the server with EMAIL_BACKEND=capture, an adapter that appends every rendered message verbatim to a file and refuses to be built at all when ENV names production. The client-side required-field guard added for #2822 deliberately stops short of this seam: a blank or whitespace-only Send Reset Link now returns before the API client is called, so there is no request for a spec here to observe and the rate-limit budget this route spends per hour is never touched. That behaviour is pinned in the Jest suite for ForgotPasswordScreen; this journey is unchanged by it and stays covered.

A user logs in and is handed a session that lives thirty days rather than an hour (#2804); a refresh rotates it, the rotated token reads their data, and the token rotated away is refused on the very next call even though its exp is weeks out. The backend suite asserts the minted lifetime and the revocation row in-process; this is the place the production client's refresh call, the jti revocation `/auth/refresh` writes, and the lookup every authenticated route performs are exercised together across the wire. The half-life renewal the client schedules against that lifetime is a timer, so it stays in the Jest suite for AuthContext.

A session whose credential expires while the user is on Habits opens the re-auth sheet over that screen: the stored token is refused and its /auth/refresh fails (#3396). The app now holds no token, so the still-mounted screen's next GET /ui-flags goes out anonymous and the real backend answers 401 not_authenticated. That 401 must not collapse the sheet to Get Started; the sheet stays open, the person signs back in from it through the real /auth/login, and lands on Habits with their seeded habit. Only the expired credential is faked in the browser; the anonymous 401 and the new session's requests reach the real server. Asserted at 390 and 1280, with the sheet's controls inside the viewport at normal and doubled text. Jest covers the controls: a genuinely anonymous session still lands on anonymous, signing out from the sheet still signs out, another account signing in from the sheet still wipes, and a not_authenticated 401 racing the expiry before the sheet renders still leaves it open.

A signed-out reader sees the editorial auth layout vertically centred when it fits, then can reach both ends of the Get Started content when the available height shrinks to a keyboard-sized viewport. Every auth route -- Get Started, Login, Signup, Forgot Password, Reset Password and Cancel Reset -- exposes the same scroll surface, and the journey finishes by creating an account through the production client so the tested surface crosses its real seam. The browser half pins actual overflow and centring geometry; the native PR evidence separately exercises iOS 18.6 at accessibility-extra-extra-extra-large because a browser cannot emulate iOS Dynamic Type.

A user taps Continue with Google and the sign-in fails on Google's side: Google refuses the redirect (a misconfigured client, a server error, a state mismatch), or on native the one-time code cannot be traded for an ID token (a refused trade or a dead network). The Google error slot then shows "Google couldn't complete that sign-in. Try again, or continue with email instead." and the button is free to retry, while a user who cancels, dismisses or declines on Google's own screen sees nothing. Uncovered because Playwright cannot drive Google's consent sheet, and every failure leg is produced inside expo-auth-session or Google's token endpoint before any request crosses our seam; pinned meanwhile by useGoogleAuth.test.tsx and the SocialAuthButtons tests.

A fresh account reads all four Welcome panels naming the journal floor, independently chosen depths, user-named habits with check-ins, and grounding or timed practices (#3103). At 390x844 and 1280x720, every body, privacy note and pager control stays in view. On a 320x568 phone and with 200% text, each panel scrolls vertically while Skip and Next/Begin remain available. Begin and Skip each hand the reader to the Journal shelf through its real GET /journal/ request. The spec awaits PATCH /ui-flags has_seen_welcome=true before reload and verifies the subsequent GET /ui-flags returns true, proving account-owned persistence. It saves panel screenshots for visual inspection.

A user first tries to create a habit whose name contains only whitespace, a NUL, zero-width text, and Unicode default-ignorables; the production client receives the stable habit_name_empty refusal, and a fresh list proves neither the habit nor its three default goals exists. A visible name wrapped in outer whitespace and a zero-width suffix is then canonicalized on the server and returned without losing its supported Unicode. The user logs 10 units under one tier with a durable operation key; replaying that exact act leaves the server at 10. Logging 5 under the next tier produces a habit-day total of 15, a signed -8 correction crosses the tier boundary to 7, and an oversized -99 correction clamps the entire habit day to 0. A final +10 leaves the freshly listed server state and streak intact. The same client reconciliation that drives the tile is pinned in habitManager.test.ts: it replaces every optimistic row for the affected day with the response's day_units, so reopen and the immediate tile agree.

A user whose additive progress has run far beyond Stretch still sees separately operable tier controls: the visual scale stops compressing before the distinct targets overlap, a long press names the negative walk-back adjustment it will make, releasing that press restores the server-backed fill, and dragging Low or Clear cannot cross the displayed Stretch marker. The current live-wire habit journey proves signed corrections and day-total reconciliation but does not operate the tile or GoalModal marker gestures in a browser, so #2814 tracks this missing seam. Pinned meanwhile by HabitUtils.test.ts for extreme and equal-adjacent marker geometry plus inverse target math, starFill.test.ts and HabitTileStarLongPress.test.tsx for over-Stretch walk-back and fill release, and GoalModal.markerDrag.test.tsx for the displayed drag ceiling and persisted target.

A user opens a habit modal and leaves the operation on + to add the entered amount, taps once for set to make the selected day's total exact, or taps again for − to subtract the entered amount. Log Units remains the only commit action. The set operation derives the signed correction from that selected calendar day's existing completions before using the ordinary append-only completion route. Uncovered because the browser habit journey logs through its API-backed seam but does not yet open GoalModal; pinned meanwhile by GoalModal.test.tsx for the operation cycle, add/subtract qualification, exact higher and lower totals, selected past-day bucketing, and reset after commit.

A user whose Journaling habit is linked to the writing timer opens its goal editor and is offered only minutes or sessions, per day or per week, under the note “Logged automatically by the timer — minutes, or one session per sitting.” A pick saves through the batch units PUT. A habit nothing is linked to keeps all twenty units. When a habit is linked elsewhere while its editor is open, the stale editor's “reps” is refused by the backend guard with a 422, the toast carries the server's reason, and the tiers return to minutes (#3154). Practice links (UserPractice.habit_id) feed the same editor through useLinkedHabitIds and are pinned by GoalModal.linkedUnits.test.tsx and useLinkedHabitIds.test.tsx.

A user opens a habit's goal editor, changes its cadence to three times per week, explicitly saves the number, and sees every tier restated in plain language. The same commit is available from Return and blur on web, iOS and Android, with the overlapping native events collapsed into one batch PUT. Uncovered because the current habits browser journey creates and checks in a habit but never opens GoalModal or changes the shared three-tier units; #2814 tracks the seam-crossing epic coverage. Pinned meanwhile by GoalModal.test.tsx for the Save/Return/blur event matrix, invalid and unchanged drafts, shared tooltip/tier copy, GoalModal.starLongPress.test.tsx for the drag-confirm copy and the long-press-fill arbitration, and — after #2884 — GoalModal.markerDrag.test.tsx for the value a marker drop actually saves, backed by markerDrag.test.ts for the drag geometry and HabitUtils.test.ts for the percent-to-target inverse. The drag writes PUT /goals/{goal_id} through the goals client, a different seam from the units batch PUT this journey's editor half uses; both are still mocked in the component lane, which is what 2814 tracks.

A user whose Lifting habit is three sessions per week logs once on Monday, rests on Tuesday, and still sees one of three rather than an empty day or a full bar. Wednesday advances the same bar to two of three, Friday fills it, the following Monday starts a new period, and a monthly habit follows its account-local calendar month. The marker, tier, colour, tooltip, and long-press fill all read the same period total. Uncovered because the current habits browser journey creates only daily goals and never opens GoalModal to persist a weekly cadence; #2814 tracks the seam-crossing epic coverage. Pinned meanwhile by HabitUtils.test.ts for ISO-week/month, timezone, DST, additive/subtractive, and rollover behavior; HabitTileTooltip.test.tsx for the rendered fraction and marker; and starFill.test.ts for the logged delta.

A user whose Lifting habit is three sessions per week met that target in each of the last two ISO weeks and has logged once so far this week. The tile, GET /habits, GET /habits/{habit_id}/stats and every check-in response all report a streak of 2 weeks: a rest day never breaks it, the still-open week is grace until it is met, and completing it makes 3 weeks. The tile, stats sheet and reminder say weeks or months instead of days. Uncovered because the current habits browser journey creates only daily goals and never persists a weekly cadence; #2814 tracks the seam-crossing epic coverage. Pinned meanwhile by one shared parity fixture (backend/tests/fixtures/streak_parity/cadence_streaks.json) evaluated by backend tests/domain/test_period_streaks.py and frontend periodStreaks.test.ts for per_day, per_week and per_month, additive and subtractive; by backend test_habit_cadence_streaks_api.py across GET /habits, stats and both check-in paths; and by HabitUtils.test.ts.

A user creates a subtractive habit that began today and has not logged the behavior. The server classifies the three-goal habit by the shared any-goal polarity rule and reports a one-day abstention streak; after a real reload, the Habits tile shows 1 DAYS — ACHIEVED TODAY!, because zero behavior is both a no-log streak day and within the clear ceiling. The browser runs in the user's America/Los_Angeles timezone, so the create/load round-trip also exercises the local calendar boundary rather than reparsing the server's date as UTC midnight.

A regular program habit appears when the program's invitation reaches it. A habit sitting on one of the ten rings waits for that ring to open -- its stage entering the range the calendar and the record between them have unlocked -- and a start date already in the past does not stand in for that (issue #2765: on an established account every start date is past, which opened every ring at once and stopped graduated unlock from tracking the user's level). A habit whose stage names no ring has no rung to wait for, so its start date is still its whole schedule. The habits list read persists the invitation as revealed exactly once; if the person then re-locks it, another read respects the decline instead of re-opening it. The server owns eligibility and its private marker, while the client renders only the reconciled revealed flag. Carryover habits and unrecommitted Metta Return releases remain outside this automatic path, and rows stamped before the stage gate was corrected are left open rather than retroactively re-locked, all pinned by the backend API suite.

A newly registered person whose live habits request succeeds with an empty collection sees an honest first-use state with an Add a habit action, never the fictional names, streaks, or completion history reserved for an explicitly configured demo build. The page-zero fallback explains the gain -- 'Choose one habit. A minute a day begins the practice; you can build from there.' -- without claiming the account's current stage or duration. The real-wire spec proves the fresh account and production client receive an empty Page; empty-state-map-copy.browser.e2e.test.ts pins the rendered gain and reachable action at phone, desktop and effective 200% zoom; habitManager.test.ts pins that the service preserves the empty list, and HabitsEmptyState.test.tsx pins every selectCopy variant with 'no pressure' rendered at most once.

A check-in tapped while the device is offline is queued on the device, and the next habits load replays that queue: an entry the server will never accept is dropped so the queue keeps draining behind it, while a dropped connection re-queues the unposted suffix intact. Covered by frontend/e2e/habits-offline-replay.browser.e2e.test.ts against the real backend. It takes the device offline with the browser context's setOffline and waits on the app's own offline banner, logs units through the goal sheet, and reads the queue straight out of the device's storage under the account-scoped key named by the device-owner stamp. Reconnecting does not replay the habit queue by itself; a habits load does. Concurrent loads share one drain. A browser case holds the original replay POST, opens Habits, queues a new tap by failing its requests, then releases the replay: the newer operation survives cleanup and reaches the real server on the next load, with one stored unit for each habit. It asserts exactly one POST /goal_completions/ per queued check-in, each carrying that entry's own Idempotency-Key, and reads the stored rows back out of band: the units total, and the local_day a same-day replay lands on. A check-in queued yesterday and replayed today, on a page clock pinned to midday in the account's zone, sends completed_on for yesterday and is stored on yesterday. A permanent rejection is a real 404 goal_not_found, produced by deleting the queued goal's habit out of band; the entry behind it still lands, and the drop is written to a bounded on-device quarantine (the most recent records only) and surfaced on the Habits screen as a count of the check-ins that could not be saved, an alert the user can dismiss and that a later load does not bring back; the quarantine is also wiped on logout. A transient failure is a harness-side abort of every attempt for one entry's key: the queue keeps exactly the unposted suffix and the next load posts only that. A server rejection with an unrecognised status that keeps recurring is retried, and given up on only after both MAX_CHECK_IN_REPLAY_ATTEMPTS counted rejections and MIN_POISON_AGE_MS since the first (#2473); it is then quarantined and surfaced like any other drop, while offline, timeout, 401 and availability failures (408, 429, 502, 503, 504) never count. The spec reaches the give-up with a harness-fulfilled 500 for one key and a seeded retry record already one refusal short of the cap and past the age floor, so the final refusal, the drain behind it and the notice are real while the week of refusals is not; the boundaries are pinned by src/features/Habits/services/__tests__/replayPolicy.test.ts. The classification is pinned by unit tests in src/features/Habits/services/__tests__/habitManager.test.ts and src/features/Habits/hooks/__tests__/useHabitActions.test.tsx, and the notice by src/features/Habits/components/__tests__/DroppedCheckInNotice.test.tsx.

In a build explicitly configured with EXPO_PUBLIC_HABIT_DEMO_MODE=true, with the habits fetch failing and no real cache, the app seeds ten demo placeholder tiles carrying fabricated ids 1-10, and those numbers are also the ids of whatever real rows the caller happens to own. A successful empty response never enters this mode. Every action on such a tile is local: revealing, reordering, renaming, changing the icon, moving the start date in the reorder modal, editing a goal or its shared units, logging a unit, opening stats, and -- the destructive one -- deleting. The tile changes or disappears in the store and nothing goes out, so a placeholder delete cannot become a DELETE against the user's own habit 3, and no "Couldn't sync" alert appears for something the user did only to themselves. Covered by frontend/e2e/habits-demo-tile.browser.e2e.test.ts, which boots its own Expo web server on port 8080 (the other DEV_ORIGINS port, so no backend change) with EXPO_PUBLIC_HABIT_DEMO_MODE=true -- the flag is inlined at bundle time, so the shared lane's server stays non-demo, which frontend/e2e/frontendEnv.ts enforces fail-closed and the lane guard confines to that one spec. It signs up for real, aborts exactly GET /habits/ on the API origin from the harness, clears the on-device habit cache, and asserts the error state beside every HABIT_DEFAULTS tile, unlocked. It then locks and unlocks all, drags a tile and moves the first habit's start date in the reorder modal, renames, changes an icon, edits a low target and the shared unit, logs a unit (seeing the sample-habits notice), opens stats (rendered locally, never stuck loading) and deletes a tile -- recording every request and asserting none of PUT/DELETE /habits/{id}, DELETE /habits/{id}/completions, PUT /habits/{id}/goals/units, PUT /goals/{id}, POST /goal_completions/ or GET /habits/{id}/stats went out (the classifier is pinned by __tests__/demoTileBrowserSupport.test.ts). RN-web's Alert is a no-op, so that request log, not the screen, is the proof no sync alert was raised. After a reload with the list still failing, every placeholder is back as seeded: today's discard behaviour, pinned as current and not decided (#2465). One control is not reachable on web: the habit settings' start-date picker renders nothing there, so the start date is moved through the reorder modal's "First habit start date". DELETE /habits/{id}/completions has no client caller and stays in the asserted-absent list only as a demo-tile guard. The same local-only rule covers every client-minted row, not just the demo family: onboarding scaffold rows and pre-sync added rows are marked hasClientMintedIds and may not put their provisional ids on the wire. A client-minted row is the user's real data, so it reaches the on-disk cache while a demo tile never does; that half, and the mixed store where the one real row still syncs, stay pinned by unit tests in src/features/Habits/services/__tests__/serverIds.test.ts, src/features/Habits/services/__tests__/habitManager.test.ts, and src/features/Habits/hooks/__tests__/useHabitActions.test.tsx.

A habit added after onboarding takes the next rung on the program cadence rather than the day it was added, so the row sits where a reorder pass would put it and carries the date its stage badge has always implied. The second half is the one that moved other screens: a row stamped today could undercut a start date the user picked in the future, because when no anchor is stored -- after a logout wipes it, or for an account that onboarded before the anchor existed -- the universal anchor Map, Practice, Course and Journal all read is re-derived as the minimum over program rows, and a today-stamped add won that minimum. The covering Playwright spec pins the browser to UTC, signs up through the UI and seeds two program rows over POST /habits/ on the rungs of an anchor thirty days in the future, then reloads so the journal derives that anchor -- which the Map confirms before anything is added: stage 2 reads Opens in 51 days. It adds a habit through the Habits drawer's Add Habit sheet and reads two things that can fail. On the wire, the sheet's POST /habits/ carries the third rung (anchor + 42 days), not today, and GET /habits/ echoes that start_date on a program row. On screen, after a real log-out from Settings -- the spec checks the stored anchor is gone -- and a log-in through POST /auth/login, the anchor is re-derived from the rows, the added one among them, and the Map still reads Opens in 51 days; a today-stamped add would make it read 21. No habit tile renders a date, the reorder modal re-lays every program row on the cadence the moment it opens, and the web date picker in habit settings renders nothing, so none of those is the observation. Pinned in process as well by src/features/Habits/services/__tests__/habitManager.test.ts (the "addHabit lays a program row on the cadence" block, which covers the stored anchor, the absent-anchor fallback, the day-one case, the carryover partition, the reload that follows the add, and the saturation past ten stages that this deliberately shares with the reorder modal).

The date the user picks in Energy Scaffolding is the day their program begins, and it stays that day. They choose it in the reorder step, the scaffold rows POST with dates laid out from it, and the reload that follows re-derives the universal anchor that Map, Practice, Course and Journal all read for the current stage and week. A habit the user brought along from before the program carries the date they actually started it, which is usually earlier than the date they picked, and it must not become the program's beginning -- otherwise bringing one habit along on day one moves every other screen back to a day the program had not started. Uncovered because this lane runs on the node environment with node_modules untransformed and cannot mount a screen at all, the same constraint already recorded on welcome.first-run-walkthrough-to-journal: driving this journey means opening the scaffolding modal, operating its date picker, and adding a habit from the carryover lap, none of which a lane that cannot render can do. Pinned meanwhile by unit tests in src/features/Habits/services/__tests__/habitManager.test.ts (the "program anchor ignores carryover habits" block, which covers the live load, the offline cache, and the reload that follows onboardingSave) and by the picker's own label in src/features/Habits/components/__tests__/OnboardingModal.step4.test.tsx. Two anchors exist and this journey watches only the client's: the server stamps its own when the progress row is created, so a user who picks a future date has one of each and they disagree until they are reconciled.

A user opens Reorder Habits and performs a real browser pointer drag across the visible carryover/program boundary. Crossing that line changes the persisted is_carryover classification; after saving, the browser walks both pages and verifies that the remaining program habit keeps the ranked Beige stage color while the moved carryover tile and its progress use the unranked Candle & Ink accent. The component suite separately pins light/dark accents, achieved-state brightening, the -10 to -1, 1–10, and later-lap markers, plus program-date recalculation and carryover-date preservation.

A user with a long habit name opens Energy Scaffolding and reaches the reorder step, where each habit is a draggable row (#3398). The covering spec signs up through the real client, seeds one habit with an 85-character name through the real API, walks review, add, both energy steps and the count warning, then measures the row in Chromium at 390px and 1280px with normal and doubled name text. Every glyph box of the name sits inside the row and the viewport, no word of the name is split across lines (on a phone the name drops to its own line under the date rather than breaking mid-word), the page never scrolls sideways, the date, icon-edit control and energy line stay inside the row without overlapping the name or each other, the energy line hangs on the date's left edge, and doubling the name adds lines without moving the date or the edit control. Saved frames are inspected by hand. Targeted text doubling does not establish physical OS zoom or native geometry.

A returning user taps Start Energy Scaffolding in Course while the Habits tab has never been opened (#3328). The handoff is consumed at once but the onboarding opens only after this account's habits have been read from the server under the live authentication session, so the review asks about the rows the user already has instead of showing the empty new-user flow. The covering spec signs up through the real client, seeds two habits over the real API, holds the cold tab's first GET /habits/ in Chromium at 390px and 1280px, and proves the modal stays closed while a waiting notice says why, then that releasing the read opens the review with both seeded rows. Controls: a rejected read with no cache keeps the handoff behind the existing error banner and opens once its Retry succeeds; a rejected read behind cached rows offers the notice's own Try again; Not now declines the held handoff and nothing opens later. The notice is measured for clipped or escaping glyphs and sideways page scroll at normal and targeted doubled text, and saved frames are inspected by hand. Account switch, A-to-B-to-A, a disabled ring and a stale earlier-session read during the hold are pinned in src/features/Habits/hooks/__tests__/useEnergyOnboardingIntent.test.ts, and the read outcome the hold keys on in the refreshHabits block of src/features/Habits/services/__tests__/habitManager.test.ts. Targeted text doubling does not establish physical OS zoom or native geometry.

A user first arrives at an empty Journal whose invitation distinguishes corpus membership from bounded reflection retrieval: with corpus sorting enabled, every eligible page not marked Intimate joins the private corpus, whether new or already written; Higher Self may draw only a few passages from it for a reflection. The Start a page action remains the same. empty-state-map-copy.browser.e2e.test.ts pins that invitation and reachable action at phone, desktop and effective 200% zoom. The Journal-wide word-wrap sweep separately proves every token in the invitation has a safe line-break opportunity at effective 200% zoom. The user first tries to save a page made only of whitespace, a zero-width mark, and a control character; the production client receives the stable journal_message_empty refusal and the live journal remains empty. They then write legitimate Unicode prose, find it in the list, and read the body back unchanged. The backend boundary suite separately sweeps spaces, tabs/newlines, controls, and zero-width-only bodies across create and edit, proving those refusals happen before a journal row, Creek write, corpus classification, pipeline run, or wallet event.

A writer saves a page, returns to the shelf, loses their connection, and opens that page anyway: the client short-circuits the GET, so the page shows its load-error banner and will not save (#2935). When the device comes back online, the real browser sees the load run again by itself, the banner clear, and the stored body appear; the writer then edits the page without reopening it, and the PATCH lands and is read back from the server. The seam suite JournalEntryScreenReconnectLoad.test.tsx pins what the browser cannot isolate: exactly one reload per offline-to-online edge and none while merely online, no duplicate or in-flight reload, a failed reload that retries only on the next edge, a fresh page that never loads, words typed while the entry was unloaded kept below the stored body and saved once, never auto-saved into a finished entry (the edit-confirm dialog says they are waiting and they save only after Edit), never saved under a looser stored tier than the one shown while typing (the entry is escalated first; page saves, the exit flush and Finish are held while it is in flight; if it fails the words stay off the page with a note and return only after a retry or the writer's own choice confirms a strict enough tier; a looser choice keeps them held), and no exit (Close, Back to reading, back gesture or hardware back) leaves held words behind without the writer's explicit choice in a Stay / Leave without them dialog, no stale pre-load debounce writing over the stored body, and no carry of those words into a different route entry. journalReconnectLoad.test.ts pins the reload gate and the carry rules term by term.

A writer sees that ordinary New entry still opens without a title, closes it, then takes the morning-pages invitation. The real browser lands on a fresh JournalEntry titled with that account/browser's local YYYY-MM-DD plus Daily Journal, and the writer can immediately replace the generated title. The shelf component test pins the exact prefillTitle navigation parameter, the tip test freezes a UTC instant across the prior-day America/Los_Angeles boundary, and the saved Journaling-practice quick-launch suite pins the same shared title contract.

A writer on a day with no review due sees the morning-pages tip with its Begin a page CTA, a quiet Don't show this again link beneath it, and an icon-only X in the card's top-right corner named Set the morning-pages tip aside (#2860). At 390x844 and 1280x720 the real browser measures the X flush with the band's top-right corner and inside it, at least 44px square, clear of the Begin a page button's box, of the never-again link's 44px-tall box and of every line of card text, and the card's label, title, body, CTA and link on one left edge, with no visible Not now. The X sets the tip aside for TODAY only, in the account's own time zone (#3005): pressing it by keyboard removes the card, lands focus on the Start a review early link rather than the page body, persists that day under the per-day set-aside key (never the retired permanent key), keeps the tip gone after a same-day reload, and brings it back after a reload with the browser clock on the next day in the account's zone. Component tests pin the close variant's accent-while-pressed tint, the begin area's corner reserve, the focus handoff's target, the Los Angeles 23:59/00:00 boundary under frozen clocks, the return on a later focus of a still-mounted shelf, and the legacy permanent flag's one-time migration.

A writer who wants no morning-pages invitation at all activates the tip's quiet Don't show this again link by keyboard, by its spoken name (Don't show this again: stop offering morning pages on the shelf), and the card goes, focus lands on Start a review early, and the device stores the permanent never-offer flag (#3005). The tip stays gone after a same-day reload and after a reload with the browser clock on the next day in the account's zone, where the X's set-aside would have lapsed. In Settings, the Journal group's Offer morning pages switch reads off, and turning it on clears that flag and today's set-aside; back on the Journal shelf the tip is offered again. Component tests pin the link's action face at body weight in soft ink, its 44dp hit area and corner reserve, the save-then-focus order, the stale-read guard, and the Settings switch's copy sweep.

A writer enters the journal's lightweight Markdown dialect, finishes the page, and sees asterisk-delimited bold text, underscore-delimited italics, <u>tag-delimited</u> underline (a retired ==equals== spelling stays literal prose), adjacent -/*/+ lines as one list block, consecutive > lines as one quote block, # to ###### headings on the read-mode type ramp (an <h1>-<h6> on web; #tag and seven hashes stay prose), 1. / 1) items numbered exactly as typed in a two-digit column, - [ ] / - [x] task items drawn as checkboxes with a checked item dimmed, and a ---, *** or ___ line as a hairline rule (*** is never a bullet). The same rendering survives a cold reload while the exact source remains stored for editing and for code-point-based marginalia and promoted-quote anchors. The browser spec crosses the real editor, create/read routes, semantic web elements, and durable journal row, entering one heading, numbered item, task and rule and reading each back after a cold reload; component coverage separately pins malformed text, literal HTML-looking prose, Unicode offsets, and anchors that cross hidden markers, including a hidden ## and - [x] prefix.

A writer sees the journal's Markdown rendered while they are still typing it -- a styled mirror over the real textarea draws bold, italics, <u>underline</u> and quote lines in place, headings at body size in faux bold, and the markers of headings, numbered items, task checkboxes and rules, block markers and delimiters dimmed rather than deleted and revealed around the caret, every style advance-neutral so no glyph drifts from under the caret -- and formats with Cmd/Ctrl+B/I/U or the toolbar above the body, below the exit row (#3250). The phone/desktop browser measures that order, unchanged Camera exit-row placement and centred Finish rail, and 44px formatting targets; the reflection quote-fold journey retains Sources in the exit row; pointer formatting still saves byte-identical Markdown after reload. Browser undo and redo take a shortcut back, pasted Markdown is kept verbatim, and the stored body stays byte-identical to what was typed, so every marginalia / promoted-quote anchor still addresses the same code points. The spec types with the keyboard, checks the title is never intercepted, lets the page save, reloads into read mode, and separately probes that clicking a mirror glyph -- on a heading and a task line too -- puts the textarea caret on that exact character at 390/768/1024/1440px in light and dark.

A writer nests a list from the keyboard: Tab indents the list item under the caret by the document's own unit, Shift+Tab outdents it, Return on an empty nested item steps out one level (and leaves the list at level 0), and Backspace at a nested item's content start steps out one level too. Tab on prose and Shift+Tab at level 0 are left to the browser, so focus always moves on. On a list line the toolbar offers Indent and Outdent. The stored body is exactly the indentation typed, and read mode draws the same nesting after a cold reload.

A writer types a fresh page and presses the always-available X before its debounced first save. The close waits for the create response before navigation lets the shelf refetch, the new page is visible immediately, and reopening it shows the exact body. A component regression test separately holds the create promise open to prove navigation ordering and verifies a rejected final write leaves the writer with the retry affordance.

A writer's page fails to save while the device is offline: an edited body and a stricter privacy tier both fail, the tier control reverts to what the server holds, and the footer says Couldn't save with a Retry. Coming back online re-sends both with no tap, the hint settles on Saved, and the server row and the reopened page carry the new body and tier. Online, a failed tier PATCH is recovered by pressing Retry. A tier looser than the one shown is never sent by a retry: it is dropped on reconnect and the page stays at its stricter tier until the writer chooses Public again. Jest seam suites (JournalEntryScreenSaveRetry, and the #2930 cases in JournalEntryScreenPrivacy, JournalEntryScreenChord and JournalEntryScreenFinish) pin the lanes the browser cannot isolate: Finish retried through the edit gate and never on reconnect, one lane's success never clearing another's failure, the single-flight create (#1144), and the retry's own single-flight.

A writer's first save of a new page, or their answer to the week's prompt, reaches the server but its answer is lost on the way back. The page cannot tell that from a save that never arrived, so it retries: first the transport (a keyed POST is retry-eligible), then the footer's Retry. Every attempt carries the one Idempotency-Key the page minted for that create, so the server answers each retry with the row it already stored rather than writing a second entry, and a lost prompt answer settles on Saved instead of being reported as the week already taken. Words typed after the lost create are PATCHed over the replayed row, so the one stored entry holds the newer text. The browser spec commits the first POST and drops its response, counting rows through the account's own API; Jest seam suites (the #2936 cases in JournalEntryScreenSaveRetry, saveFinishedEntry and JournalPhotographScreen) pin what the browser cannot isolate: a stricter tier re-asserted on the replayed row, a failed reconcile that leaves the page id-less, the photograph capture's own key, and a replayed answer holding older words staying honest as week-taken.

A writer opens a fresh Journal page whose title occupies one line before they type. A long title can still wrap visually, pasted line breaks collapse to spaces, and Return moves the caret into the body without becoming stored title data. Closing crosses the production client and create route, and the returned durable row carries the exact single-line title; schema tests separately pin the server-side defence for non-UI create and update callers.

A reader opens a finished entry, clicks through the one-time promote explainer a fresh account meets first (Choose the passage), sees the caret-hidden selection field light its accent focus rule on focus in place of the browser ring (#2952, WCAG 2.4.7), uses a real mouse selection to promote part of its text, sees the notice name where it went (Promoted — find it any time under Promoted quotes), sees the saved highlight after a cold reload, and removes it again. The journey crosses the rendered selection affordance, production promotions client, ownership-scoped routes, and durable quote row instead of proving the API in isolation.

The first time a reader taps Promote a quote, a note opens instead of the selection field: titled Promote a quote, it says a promoted passage waits among the sources of a review that covers the week it was written (what GET /reflections/sources does: a pending quote rides with its source entry, not with whichever review comes next) and can be seen any time under Promoted quotes in the Journal menu, with a real, unticked Don’t show this again checkbox and two arms whose rendered boxes are the same size on one row. Not now closes it with no selection field and nothing stored. Asked again, the reader ticks the box and chooses the passage; the selection field takes focus (the Promote button has unmounted with the read controls, so focus would otherwise fall to the page). The reader promotes a passage over the real route and the notice reads Promoted — find it any time under Promoted quotes in a polite live region. The dismissal is written to this account's scoped key (#u<id>), the Journal menu's Promoted quotes door lists the quote under Not yet in a review, and after a cold reload the next Promote a quote goes straight to a focused selection field. Not asserted in the browser, and pinned only by Jest: the press that lands before the stored flag has loaded waiting for it, a second account on the same device still seeing the note, and the iOS VoiceOver announcement. The in-sheet Promote a passage from this source opener in a review's sources panel is deliberately not gated by the note.

A reader on a phone opens an entry several screens long, taps Promote a quote, and selects a passage near its end. The mirrored field wears no browser focus ring and grows to its text instead of becoming an inner scroll pane, and the preview / Promote / Cancel footer stays pinned at the foot of the viewport (web position: sticky) while the body scrolls, so the confirm is in reach without scrolling past the whole entry. The browser spec seeds and finishes a 121-line entry over the API, opens it from the shelf at 390x844, clicks through the one-time promote explainer, and asserts the field has outline-style none, no inner scroll (scrollHeight <= clientHeight) and a height over three viewports; with the field's top at the top of the screen, the footer and Promote selection are in the viewport and pinned over the field. It then scrolls the closing line clear of the footer, drags a real mouse selection over it, and promotes it over POST /journal/{entry_id}/promote, whose stored anchor_text equals the preview. Native, where the footer stays in flow, is pinned by QuoteSelectionSurface.test.tsx and readingSurfaceStyles.test.ts.

On any day, not only inside a review composer, a writer opens the Journal drawer's 'Promoted quotes' door (a door with no count) and sees every quote they have promoted, grouped by status: 'Not yet in a review (n)' above 'Used in a review (m)', each header carrying the server's total for its own section. A quote seeded through the real promote route near the end of a long finished page is listed verbatim with its source title; tapping it opens that page in read mode scrolled to the passage, which is underlined and asserted in the viewport. Back on the screen, Remove asks first, the confirmed remove issues DELETE /promotions/{promotion_id}, and after a cold reload the screen shows the exact empty copy and GET /promotions returns nothing. Not asserted in the browser, and pinned only by Jest and pytest: the Write a review picker hand-off, per-section paging, the revert-in-place of a refused remove, the stale and deleted-review captions, refetch on refocus, and the cross-tenant and soft-delete exclusions of GET /promotions.

A writer opens Prompts from the Journal homepage shortcut or the shared primary shelf with its Bell icon. Both Journal and Prompts retain headline tiles. Journal has no stage, return, review, morning-page or voice cards. Prompts shows the writing invitation, ring-gated Return and invitations, stage prompts, and voice cards. Clearing a stage prompt calls the real dismiss route; on return to Journal its quiet Prompts count drops by one. Clearing all active cards leaves Nothing waiting. Past prompts and set-aside cards remain browseable. Screenshots cover phone, desktop and 200% zoom.

A due weekly review is opened from the Journal shelf, saved with its hierarchical identity (tag hierarchical_reflection, level week, scope key c1:w1), closed, and reopened as an ordinary saved entry. Its Sources affordance survives that reopen, and the panel names THAT review's own period -- read from the window the sources endpoint declares it filtered on -- so a reopen can never quietly present another review's material. Selecting a pending promoted quote folds it into the body, autosaves the reflection, and marks the quote included on the server. The spec drives the WEEK level only and asserts no title text. Review titles in the program's words are asserted elsewhere: the weekly titles under journal.review-from-the-shelf-cta, the section and course invitations and titles under journal.section-and-course-review-invitations; the stage invitation is pinned only by Jest. The sheet renders each source body through the journal Markdown model -- a '**Me:**' speaker prefix reads as bold 'Me:' and no raw marker ever appears in the collapsed excerpt or the expanded body -- and closes with an icon-only X whose accessible name is 'Done'. That the body grows to hold folded quotes at phone width, instead of painting them over the footer and rail, is asserted under journal.fold-selected-promoted-quotes (#3001).

A writer composing a due weekly review opens Sources, taps 'Select quotes', and the pending quotes become checkboxes whose state the browser reads from aria-checked. With nothing checked the fixed action reads disabled (aria-disabled). Two of three quotes promoted from one source are checked out of order; the action, which sits outside the scroll and stays in the viewport, reads exactly 'Fold 2 quotes into this review'. One press splices both as Markdown blockquotes attributed to the source title, in the order they sit in the source, one blank line apart, after the writer's own text; the review autosaves to 'Saved' and the server holds that exact body; exactly one PATCH /promotions/{promotion_id} per checked quote names the review's id, and the folded rows read as folded (aria-disabled). From the review's own Journal drawer the Promoted quotes screen then reads 'Not yet in a review (1)' and 'Used in a review (2)'; there 'Select quotes' turns the waiting quote into a checkbox, the fixed footer action reads 'Fold 1 quote into this review', and pressing it returns to the review, which folds that quote in once (each passage appears exactly once in the saved body) and marks it included on the review; the screen then reads 'Not yet in a review (0)' and 'Used in a review (3)'. At a 390x844 phone viewport, after a long typed opening and a two-quote fold with no keystroke after it, the body textarea reaches the last folded line the mirror draws, and the save footer and the Finish rail start at or below the textarea's bottom -- a value written from the app re-measures the field just as typing does, so folded text never paints over them (#3001); Sources is an icon in the entry's exit row above the page, not on the rail (#3002). The toolbar leads that body taller than the phone (#3250): scrolled back into view, it bolds a word the writer typed and selected at the end of the text. When a folded quote's inclusion mark fails, at 390x844 both normally and at effective 200%, the warning and Try again control remain entirely above the idle timer dock, and the browser hit-tests the retry where it is drawn. Pinned only by Jest, not asserted in the browser: one body change and one entry write per batch whatever its size; the partial-failure retry re-marking only the refused quotes without splicing again; a failed mark's warning kept per quote, so another quote's overlapping successful fold never clears it and Try again re-marks only that quote; a quote removed meanwhile (its PATCH answers 404 promotion_not_found) retiring from the warning and the panel, and a retry marking before it splices so a removed quote's words are never put back (#2754); the duplicate-press and per-quote in-flight guards; identical blocks written once; Select all / Clear all, and on the screen Select all covering only the loaded rows with a visible note while older quotes remain; the selection surviving a resize across the side-pane breakpoint; the exact caret placements; the screen's 'Write a review with N quotes' arm (the review picker opens the chosen review, new or continued, which folds the selection in once after it hydrates); the hand-off token that only travels from a review being written; and a selection addressed to another page being left alone.

A writer composing a due weekly review opens Sources beside a week of long dailies and browses deep into the feed. The panel's heading -- the 'Sources' title, the period and the icon-only X named 'Done' -- stays fixed above a scroll that holds only the quotes and the feed, so at 390x844 and 1280x720 the X is still in the viewport and inside the panel after scrolling to the end, and it is at least 44x44. On a wide screen (1240 and up) the pane sits beside the writing sheet, never stacked full-width beneath it, and the entry body keeps a readable width and the sheet most of the height; narrower, a bounded sheet capped at the content width opens over the page. On the phone sheet the X, Escape and a tap on the backdrop each close only the panel, and after each focus returns to the Sources toggle; on the wide pane Escape does the same. Opened from the keyboard -- the toggle sits in the exit row above the editor (#3002) -- the pane and the sheet each put focus on their X, and Enter there closes the panel and hands focus back to the toggle. The route stays and the draft is untouched. Escape pressed while typing in the entry body belongs to the editor: the pane stays open and the writer keeps focus and keeps typing. The writer keeps typing, the page autosaves to 'Saved', and the server holds the continued text on the same entry id. At 390, 768, 1024 and 1440 nothing overflows horizontally, an expanded source stays readable, and closing gives the editor back its width. When a source enters quote selection, 'Promote selection' and 'Cancel' stay inside the panel at 390x844 and 1280x720. Not asserted in the browser, and pinned only by Jest: the Android hardware back button (the sheet's Modal request, the wide pane's BackHandler, which stands down while another screen covers the entry so back pops that screen), the expanded rows and in-progress selection surviving a resize across the side-pane breakpoint, and the native bound on the selection field.

A writer types formatted Unicode into the live editor -- a decomposed accent, a ZWJ emoji sequence the server strips, bold typed key by key, italics, underline, an escaped marker, a nested bullet, a leading newline and trailing spaces -- and finishes. Read mode promotes into the body the server STORED, not the typed one, and a selection's trailing space never reaches the stored span, so anchor_end - anchor_start equals the length of anchor_text. A resonance pass anchors a margin note. Two quotes folded into the due week review render as quote blocks in the live mirror at once, with exactly one blank line between them. The source is then edited before every anchor by typing formatting and by a list indent; on reopen the pending quote and the note each still address exactly their own text at the new code-point offset, and the folded quotes (whose offsets the server freezes) are listed apart rather than washed over other words. The review still renders both blocks after reopening.

On a wide read view (>= 600px) each margin note sits beside the passage it annotates rather than stacking from the top of the column: a long page given two resonance passes (the stub quotes the last sentence, so the second pass follows an appended sentence) opens with both notes far down, the first level with its highlight and each at the top computeMarginSlots gives its measured anchor, within a pixel. The two passages share a line, so the second note is pushed below the first by at least the margin gap, in document order. The margin column grows to hold the lowest note, which hangs past the end of the writing, and after scrolling journal-page-scroll to its end that note is wholly on screen -- the column stays inside the page's one shared scroll surface, never a scroller of its own. At 390px the margin stacks under the writing and keeps its document-order flow, no slot absolutely positioned. A refused check-off (the accept route answered 500) raises the margin's error banner above the notes, moving the stream without resizing it: the note is re-placed against its passage, and since the banner pushed the stream past that passage the note is held at the stream's top, clear of the banner. Pinned only by Jest: completion suggestions and undrawn (stale or overlap-skipped) notes trailing the anchored ones in creation order, a non-finite measurement trailing, the flow layout until every slot is measured, edit mode staying in flow, and a re-measure on the page's own layout. On web, explicit passage taps reveal and select the corresponding note before opening its essay, while selecting a margin note reveals and underlines its exact passage without opening an essay; a separate Open note action retains keyboard access. A long phone page proves both off-screen directions with smooth scrolling and reduced-motion jumps. Notes and their actions are inspected at 390px and 1280px with normal and doubled rendered text, including horizontal glyph bounds and 44px Open controls. A real edit that breaks the anchor keeps its note visibly stale and openable without a wrong-passage jump; unit cases additionally cover stale metadata lag, obsolete page objects, cancellation and code-point offsets. The page has one scroller and navigation has no scroll-follow feedback listener (#2893). Native alignment and navigation parity remain follow-up work with #2985.

In Prompts, a due review offers Write your Weekly Review and opens a correctly titled scoped page. On a day nothing is due, Morning Pages and the persistent early-review card appear together. At 390px and 1280px, the browser verifies the review card matches Morning Pages' raised surface, warm left rule and rounded corners, stays within the viewport, contains the two-sentence explanation and a minimum 44px Start a review early action, and contains the expanded scope picker. The explanation describes carrying daily quotes, lessons, patterns and emotional experiences into learnings across week, stage, trimester and course. Choosing Weekly Review creates and saves c1:w2 through the real API; returning and choosing Continue reopens the same entry with the same body and no duplicate. The spec attaches card screenshots at both widths. At both widths, keyboard dismissal moves focus to Bring reviews back, the decline survives reload, explicit restoration returns focus to Start a review early, and declining another writing card still focuses the restore control when early reviews are hidden. Unit tests pin account isolation, saved-state failure handling, stale reads and writes, and exclusion from the Journal prompt count after decline. Component tests additionally cover due-review dismissal, loading/failure, picker refocus and the keyboard focus handoff from declined Morning Pages to the card action. Section and course invitations are covered by journal.section-and-course-review-invitations.

A writer who finished the 36-week arc and began again reopens a review from their FIRST pass, at any level of the cadence -- a week, a stage, a section of three stages, or the whole course. The sources feed serves that cycle's own dailies, windowed against the anchor that cycle was lived under and clamped at the local midnight the loop happened, so the two laps abut rather than overlap and no entry from the new cycle appears under the old review's heading. A cycle whose anchor was destroyed by begin-again before this was fixed says it can't tell which dates the review covered, rather than implying nothing was written then. The spec pins the browser to UTC, rewinds the anchor 230 days (20 days into stage 10) with tests.e2e.program_anchor, and lets a real GET /stages/program-calendar read record stage 10 in cycle 1; it then POSTs begin-again to the real route (the Map offers the button only at 100% stage-10 progress, which no lane writer produces) and asserts cycle 2 with cycle 1's anchor retained. With a finished first-pass daily (backdated 120 days), a DRAFT c1:course review and a finished cycle-2 daily that GET /reflections/sources for c2:w1 does serve, reopening the c1:course review from the shelf and opening Sources shows the first-pass daily and never the cycle-2 one; on the wire the window ends at the local midnight of the loop day, short of the course's natural 252 days, and the panel's period label names that declared window. With the anchor nulled by the out-of-band forget-past-anchor arrange (the state a pre-#2894 loop left), the feed is anchor_status unrecorded with no bounds and the panel shows the 'can't tell which dates this review covered' copy, with no period label and no empty-period copy. Sources is a writing-only door (#3002/#3004): it is opened on a draft review, and a FINISHED first-pass review opens to read with no Sources until Edit is pressed and confirmed. Pinned only by pytest and Jest: the week, stage and section levels, multi-loop index padding, and a review spanning weeks never lived (test_reflections_window.py, tests/domain/test_cycle_calendar.py, test_stages_api.py, ReflectionSourcesPanel.test.tsx).

On the last day of every third stage the Journal shelf offers a Section Review named after the Wavelength turn it closes (Red at stage 3, Green at 6, Ultraviolet at 9), and on the program's final day it offers the Course Review, whose sources decompose into the three sections plus the tenth stage that no section covers. Both moments became reachable only with issue #2866 -- before it, a third stage closed as a plain stage review and the final week closed as a "program" review. The spec pins the browser to UTC and rewinds the anchor in DAYS AGO, not 1-based program days: 62 days back is program day 63, the last of stage 3, where GET /reflections/due names section c1:x1, the shelf's one call to write is 'Write your Section Review' with 'Section Review -- Red' in its accessible name, the opened page is titled 'Section Review -- Red', and the saved page is exactly one c1:x1 entry tagged hierarchical_reflection at level section. 251 days back is program day 252, the final day, where c1:course is due: with finished c1:x1, c1:x2 and c1:x3 reviews, a finished daily backdated into week 1 and a finished daily written today (stage 10, week 36), GET /reflections/sources?level=course returns exactly the three section reflections then the stage-10 daily, in that server order, and never the week-1 daily that section 1 stands in for; the shelf offers 'Write your Course Review', the page is titled 'Course Review', and its Sources panel shows each section row under the 'Section reflection' eyebrow, the stage-10 daily, and no week-1 daily. The panel re-sorts the feed by time, so the decomposition order is asserted on the wire, not on screen. Pinned only by Jest and pytest: the Green and Ultraviolet sections and the stage CTA (JournalPrimaryInvitation.test.tsx), the whole-curriculum walk (tests/domain/test_reflection_hierarchy.py), the timezone-local day count and the period label (test_reflections_api.py, test_reflections_window.py).
A writer deletes one page from the shelf, the server stops serving it, and another account cannot delete it for them.

A vault-bound writer's Personal page reaches their connected Creek vault, and the vault, not the app provider, answers its resonance pass (#3061). The writer asks for a first letter on that note, and the vault writes it through Creek's letters capability, storing it as an AI-attributed Voice Draft in one call (#3203): the letter is the vault's own text and no Voice Draft PUT carries it. The writer then deletes the page. The first content-free Voice Draft retraction fails at the real HTTP boundary, so Adepthood answers with its stable retryable vault_withdrawal_pending and keeps the page visible instead of claiming success while derived plaintext remains. Repeating the same action after Creek recovers confirms both the AI-attributed draft and the journal replica absent before the local page answers 404. The lane uses the production client and an out-of-process contract fake that records only opaque ids, tiers, actions, and digests; no journal or generated prose returns through its control surface.

A writer whose page reached a Creek vault they have since replaced or disconnected deletes that page (#3094, #3098). The DELETE never dials the new vault and answers a 503 that says, in content-free relational terms, where the copy is: vault_withdrawal_previous_vault or vault_withdrawal_disconnected_vault. The shelf keeps the page, says why, and offers reconnect first (opening vault settings) or "I can't reach it", which calls POST /journal/{entry_id}/erase-locally: the page is erased here -- gone from read, list and export -- a content-free unconfirmed obligation is kept bound to the old vault, and the plain receipt says a copy may remain there and must be deleted there; nothing reports it withdrawn. Reconnecting the old vault later lets the background sweep confirm and clear the obligation. A page copied to a vault before destination binding (#3095) recorded no vault at all: the connected vault is still asked but its answer is never trusted, so the DELETE (and an Intimate reclassification) answers vault_withdrawal_unrecorded_vault, the shelf tells the person plainly that a copy made before October 7, 2026 may remain in a vault they connected earlier, and "I can't reach it" erases the page here with an unconfirmed obligation bound to no vault -- a receipt naming unrecorded_vault that no vault can ever clear. Uncovered because no lane spec yet drives two vault connections for one account against the out-of-process contract fake; pinned meanwhile by backend/tests/test_journal_unreachable_vault.py, backend/tests/test_journal_delete_completion.py, backend/tests/test_vault_destination_binding.py and the Jest suites JournalShelfScreenDelete.test.tsx, JournalEntryScreenPrivacy.test.tsx and api/__tests__/journalErasure.test.ts.

While the operator's PRIVACY_SUSPEND_VAULT_SEND switch is on, a writer with a connected Creek vault saves or edits a Personal page (#3107). The page is saved locally; the vault adapter refuses the ingest before the wire, so the write is recorded as suspended -- not degraded -- and the page owes nothing: no vault destination is bound and no VAULT_WRITE lineage shadow is logged. Deleting that page later completes at once (204, no withdrawal dial, no obligation row), even if the vault has since been disconnected. Once the switch is lifted, the next save really sends, binds the destination and records the shadow exactly once. A first essay letter asked for under the switch is the same (#3122): the letter is kept locally, and its Voice Draft mirror leaves no VoiceDraftRetraction intent and no VOICE_DRAFT_MIRROR shadow, while a mirror PUT that was dialled and failed (a 5xx or a lost acknowledgement) keeps both. Uncovered because no lane spec drives the operator switch against the out-of-process contract fake; pinned meanwhile by backend/tests/test_vault_destination_binding.py, backend/tests/test_privacy_lineage.py, backend/tests/test_creek_vault_write.py and backend/tests/test_voice_draft_mirror_suspension.py.

While the operator's PRIVACY_SUSPEND_EXTERNAL_AI switch is on, a writer whose non-intimate page screens as acute distress asks for resonance (#3120). The local, model-free distress screen runs before the suspension refusal, so the answer is the care-only 200 -- the care surface, no marginalia, unspent balances -- with no provider built or dialled, no charge, no generation slot and no usage row. A page that is not flagged still gets the 503 ai_suspended refusal. Uncovered because no lane spec drives the operator switch; pinned meanwhile at the route by backend/tests/incident/test_privacy_suspension.py.

A vault-bound writer whose Personal page has reached their connected Creek vault, and whose first letter on its margin note the vault itself wrote and stored as a Voice Draft (#3203), chooses Intimate for that page (#3060, #3077). The stricter tier is committed locally whatever the vault says. When the first content-free Voice Draft retraction fails at the real HTTP boundary, the PATCH answers the stable retryable 503 vault_withdrawal_pending -- the existing privacy control keeps Intimate selected and offers a retry -- instead of a 200 while the AI-authored draft is still in the vault. Each further choice of Intimate re-sends the owed DELETE from a durable, content-free obligation row and succeeds only once the vault confirms both the draft and the journal replica absent; a further choice once confirmed sends nothing. The lane uses the production client against the out-of-process contract fake.

Someone in the middle of a stage opens the Journal shelf and sees that stage's whole prompt set, each with the cadence the curriculum states for it, then taps one and writes against that prompt rather than against whichever question the week happened to draw. The seam is the ordinal: the page carries prompt_ordinal into the respond call, and the server decides whether that ordinal is one the stage actually carries. The second seam is the one-response-per-week rule: uq_promptresponse_user_week means a week holds a single response whichever prompt it answers, so the shelf stops offering a tap once this week's is written and the entry page says so if a save is refused anyway. Uncovered because no lane spec talks to the prompts routes yet, and a mocked client agrees with itself about the ordinal check, the stage's unlock gate, and the unique constraint -- the three things only the server can refuse.

A writer opens a page they finished days ago, asks for its resonance, and the reading lands in the margin against the words they actually wrote. The unhappy half is part of the journey rather than an edge case: a pass can legitimately keep nothing -- the model declines, or every quote it offers is a paraphrase that will not anchor -- and what the writer must never get is the outcome that was reported here, a button that visibly does nothing. So the journey ends either in a persisted note or in a sentence saying why there is none, with the charge reversed. Every note the stub writes is recorded and returned as a demo (source demo, paid_by free) and its unit is handed back (#3062); a real provider's pass whose charge is kept cannot be reached on this lane and is declared as journal.real-provider-pass-keeps-its-charge. Both endings are driven here against the configured default provider, which is the stub (BOTMASON_PROVIDER unset: no key, no network, no third party), so the route, the wallet, the anchoring and the rows are all real and only the model's sentences are canned; the stub declines exactly when the page gives it no sentence to copy, which is how the lane reaches the second ending. The spec also pins the privacy floor across the wire: an intimate page is answered before any provider is constructed, keeps no notes, and is not charged. What is NOT claimed is that any of it renders -- this lane runs on the node environment with node_modules untransformed and cannot mount JournalEntryScreen at all, the constraint recorded on welcome.first-run-walkthrough-to-journal. The margin's placement and its empty-state copy stay pinned by the Jest specs beside the screen; what crosses the seam here is that the note the margin will draw is one the server kept, anchored to characters the writer wrote. A pass also never runs over a copy whose latest write failed (#2980), nor while offline-typed words are held off the page (#2935): the screen's pass writer answers 'not saved' rather than the entry id, so nothing is generated or charged, the footer's Couldn't save / Retry keeps the save, the margin says the page has not saved (never 'write a little first'), and the next press after the save lands runs exactly one pass -- pinned client-side by frontend/src/features/Journal/__tests__/JournalEntryScreenResonanceDurable.test.tsx, since this lane cannot mount the screen.

A writer who has connected a vault -- ready, still provisioning, or with a stored host this server will not dial, or the deployment vault's bound owner -- asks for resonance. Their pass is answered by the vault or by nothing (#3061): a vault with nothing usable to say is a refunded zero-note pass with the server's own explanation; a vault that cannot answer (down, refusing, timing out, unreadable, a malformed capability handshake, no reflect capability, an unrecognized tier) is a refunded, retryable 503 reflection_source_unavailable whose margin copy says nothing was charged and the entry is saved; a locally distress-flagged entry gets the care surface alone; and completion detection, inside the pass and on the standalone route, answers checked: false. In none of those is the app's own model provider dialled, whatever BYOK key the request carries -- nor, when the writer reconnects or disconnects their vault while a pass is in flight, is that pass re-sent to the new vault or the app provider. Still uncovered as a journey: the wire lane's bound vault owner now crosses the real seam on the happy arm only -- journal-vault-withdrawal.e2e.test.ts asserts its margin note is the lane vault's own answer to POST /v1/reflections -- while none of the fail-closed arms above is driven over the wire yet; the out-of-process fake Creek vault (fakeCreekVault.mjs) is their future home. Pinned meanwhile at the route by backend/tests/security/test_vault_boundary_no_fallback.py, structurally by backend/tests/security/test_app_provider_construction_chokepoint.py, and client-side by useResonance.test.tsx and errorMessages.test.ts. The timing-out arm moved with Geoffe-Ga/Creek-Vault#1903 step 2: the pass's enforced ceiling from request to first byte, the vault's model wake included, was the pooled client's ten-second read phase and is now the thirty-second whole-request deadline, so a vault that takes between ten and thirty seconds to answer now returns a reflection where it previously returned the refunded 503 above. Which side of that line a real vault falls on is exactly what is still uncovered as a journey -- no lane drives a reflection slow enough to straddle it -- and the widened budgets themselves are pinned instead at the adapter, by test_http_reflect_runs_under_the_widened_phase_budgets in backend/tests/test_creek_vault_http_client.py.

A writer who has connected a vault asks for a margin note's letter, photographs a page, or -- having agreed to the corpus -- saves, edits, or grants consent over writing they already had. None of those is answered by the app's own model provider, whatever BYOK key the request carries (#3061, #3156). A letter is written by the vault when it advertises letters (#3203), charged one unit whatever key header rides along; a vault that does not, or cannot be reached, or gives no verified letter, fails closed with a 503 reflection_source_unavailable before any charge (or refunded after one), with the note's essay left empty so a later ask can still buy one (a letter already bought still reopens free). No vault advertises a classification adepthood may call or a transcription today, so a page is the same 503 before the image, payer, or wallet gate, and a save or edit stores no corpus fragment while a consent grant's sweep stops before its first offer and leaves every entry unmarked, so the writing is not demoted for a refusal about the account. The vault-written letter is asserted across the wire, against the lane's vault owner, inside journal.withdraw-connected-vault-copy and journal.intimate-reclassification-withdraws-copies. This journey stays uncovered as a whole because no lane spec drives the corpus or transcription routes for a vault-bound writer, and the transcription capture itself is uncovered (#2768). Pinned at the route by backend/tests/security/test_vault_bound_essay_and_corpus.py and backend/tests/test_vault_written_letters.py, each refusal with an app-provider counterweight that watches the same dial spy fire, and structurally by backend/tests/security/test_app_provider_construction_chokepoint.py, which fails any ungated provider dial or classifier call.

A vault-bound writer opens a margin note the lane vault wrote, sees the priced offer, and asks for its first letter; the lane vault answers that one request with Creek's own published letters care-escalation cell, read verbatim from the vendored bundle (#3380). The essay route answers 200 with essay null and care set to adepthood's own reviewed care surface -- the same domain.care payload a resonance escalation returns -- and the modal renders exactly that through CareSupportNote: the server's heading, message and resources, with no blank-letter error, no retry nudge, and none of Creek's own care prose. The ask costs nothing (GET /user/usage is unchanged). Because the vault stored no letter, the staged Voice Draft intent is released (#3379): after a reload the same note is offered again, and the next ask is written by the vault. Captured at 390px and 1280px, normal and doubled text. Pinned at the route by backend/tests/test_vault_written_letters.py (care surface, refund, released intent, retry to a newly bound vault, an owed earlier offer kept owed) and in Jest by ResonanceEssayModal.test.tsx and resonance.test.ts.

A writer's page screens as acute distress, and the resonance pass returns the care surface beside the reading (NORTH-STAR §10). The card opens on a short heading -- "You're not alone in this" -- with the four resources in server order, the 988 line first and Crisis Text Line second; the 988 row is asserted as a compact row that joins name and contact on one line and still says what the line is. An icon-only X in the card's corner removes the whole card: the journal page rises by at least the card's height less the one "Support options" line that stays in its place, and keyboard focus lands on that line instead of dropping to the page. That line restores all four resources in a single tap and puts focus back inside the card. Dismissing again and running a second distress-flagged pass re-shows the full card, because the dismissal is held in memory against that one care payload. Settings -> Support & care still lists all four resources afterwards. The care copy is the server's own reviewed payload crossing the real route on the lane's stub provider -- nothing about it is mocked -- and the page's rise and the focus handoff are measured in the browser because Jest has no layout or DOM focus.

A writer opens a finished page and presses Get Resonance for the first time. The press opens a disclosure before any request leaves the browser: what a pass does, that the entry's text, up to three other pieces of the writer's own writing, short excerpts of earlier letters, and the names and units of their habits and practices are sent to an AI model, and who pays. With no key, the rendered copy uses the deployment-served monthly cap and never promises that the allowance is free. The writer backs out, saves their own key through Settings, reopens the same page, and now sees that the key pays and neither BotMason bucket will move. Continue sends exactly one real request through the screen and production API to the lane's provider; its deterministic credit refusal proves the BYOK header arrived, while GET /user/usage proves both BotMason buckets stayed unchanged. The dismissal is then taken and the next press goes straight through without silently switching payer. Counted requests and server state keep the journey non-vacuous: a dialog-only assertion could pass while charging too early or charging both payers. This has to be the browser lane because the claim spans rendered presses and device key storage. Per-account namespacing of the dismissal flag remains pinned in the Jest specs beside the screen.

A writer can open API-key settings from the journal entry's exit row and return to the exact editor with its title and body intact. When the account has neither a monthly message nor an offering and no device key, Get Resonance opens a refill invitation naming the reset date instead of a disabled spend disclosure; its Add your API key arm reaches the same settings screen and returns without losing the draft. A second browser account makes the usage read stale, takes and dismisses the ordinary spend disclosure, and receives a real-shaped 402 from the pass: the refill invitation still replaces the old dialog, proving the dismissal flag cannot suppress the recovery path. A third holds the initial wallet response while the writer uses the live Settings form to save a lane key, then proves the mounted entry publishes only the new BYOK payer when that obsolete zero-wallet response arrives. A fourth holds an accepted resonance POST, opens and saves API-key settings, then releases a key-required 402 and proves the obsolete request cannot portal a funding invitation over Settings or the preserved entry. The browser intercepts only the deterministic wallet arrangements and funding failures; navigation, editor state, key storage/context, modal decisions, API client parsing, and request count all run through production code.

A note's first letter is a charged depth under the owner-ratified launch economy (#623): one wallet unit to write it, nothing to reopen it. Opening a note with no letter shows an offer, not a request: what a letter is, that the entry goes to an AI model, the price for the payer in force (the writer's own key, the monthly allowance by its served cap, or an offering), and equal-weight Ask for the letter / Not now arms. Only Ask sends POST /journal/marginalia/{marginalia_id}/essay, with price_acknowledged: true. Across the real wire, a server-paid ask without the acknowledgement is refused 409 essay_price_unacknowledged and moves neither the wallet nor its audit trail; the acknowledged ask takes its monthly unit before the dial and, because every lane serves the stub provider whose letter is a labelled demo (#3062), hands it back in the same commit (spend_monthly then refund_demo, the letter's essay_source demo), and its answer carries the same remaining_messages, remaining_balance and monthly_reset_date that GET /user/usage then reports; a real provider's letter whose charge is kept is no longer reachable on this lane and is declared as journal.real-provider-pass-keeps-its-charge; reopening the cached letter, acknowledged or not, is free. Pinned by Jest rather than this lane: the offer's copy and a11y, no ask on open, a cached letter opening straight to the letter, and an essay 402 routing to the pass's refill dialog. Pinned by the backend suite rather than this lane: the exhausted-wallet 402 before any provider call, and refunds for failed and empty letters.

A writer requests resonance through the real screen, reads independently validated notes and completion receipts plus the live reported payment route, and reopens the page after reload (#3206, Refs #3062). The real stub route persists demo source/provider/model/version and leaves the wallet unchanged; the real bound-owner route talks to the isolated Creek contract process and persists Creek source/provider with no model identity. The demo letter is explicitly requested over the real essay endpoint and appears on the real Voice Drafts shelf. Live payer data vanishes on reload while each stored note keeps its own recorded tuple. Separately labelled controlled-response cases prove client rendering for app-provider, legacy/missing, future-version, contradictory provider/demo-payer, and malformed mixed-operation metadata without losing prose; letters use only essay_source.
