Notes and completion can name different reported providers, and checked=false with a non-none receipt denotes an unconfirmed attempted check rather than an unsent check. All three supported payment-route labels are driven by response metadata, never inferred from a stored key or connection. Long reported model identities wrap at phone/desktop widths with 200% receipt text. Controlled cases do not prove third-party inference, real billing, backend persistence of their overrides, local models, attestation or custody; source identity is reported disclosure. Unsupported device-direct receipt contracts remain unrecorded pending their separate owner decision.

The happy bound-Creek receipt and reload label are covered by journal.margin-note-source-survives-reload using the isolated Creek contract process (#3206). Remaining uncovered across the wire: a vault that answers with no usable notes still names its source beside the real refunded empty-pass reason, and unavailable/fail-closed source paths render their error without inventing model identity or billing. Controlled UI response cases are client validation evidence, not proof of these backend outcomes. Backend inference_provenance and vault-boundary tests pin those semantics; no physical local-model or custody proof is claimed. Refs #3062 and journal.vault-bound-reflection-fails-closed.

A writer's resonance pass, or a note's first letter, answered by the app's real model provider is labelled as such and keeps its wallet unit, while a demo (stub) answer is refunded (#3062). Every lane serves the stub provider, so since demo answers stopped being billed the charged-and-kept half of journal.ask-for-resonance and journal.told-what-an-essay-costs-before-it-charges is unreachable from any spec. The backend suite pins it (backend/tests/test_inference_provenance.py, and the charge assertions in test_resonance_endpoints.py and test_essay_endpoint.py that now answer as a real provider).

Resonance or essay refused by a generation guardrail shows honest copy and costs nothing (#623). Under the owner-ratified limits (decision record §1: maximum 5 LLM generations/minute/user, maximum 2 concurrent generations/user, a configurable launch ceiling of 100 charged generations/day/user), a pass or a first letter asked for while two of the writer's generations are in flight is refused 429 generation_in_progress, and one past today's ceiling 429 daily_generation_limit_reached with Retry-After to the next UTC midnight; neither charges the wallet, writes an audit row or dials a provider. The margin line and the essay modal announce the refusal's own copy (wait for the one in flight; resets at midnight UTC), never the 402 refill invitation, and the essay modal offers no retry for the daily one. Uncovered because no e2e seam can put the account into either state: the daily ceiling counts walletaudit rows and the e2e lane has no database-seeding seam (the frontend has no pg client), lowering BOTMASON_DAILY_GENERATION_CEILING on the shared e2e server would refuse every other resonance spec, and holding two generations open needs a provider double the server lane does not expose. Pinned meanwhile by backend tests/routers/test_generation_guardrails_api.py (every refusal's 429, no charge, no dial, slot release on every exit) and by Jest: ResonanceEssayModal.test.tsx, JournalEntryScreenResonanceExplainer.test.tsx, generationRefusal.test.ts and errorMessages.test.ts.

A writer asks for resonance on a short saved entry that explicitly says they completed a tracked habit. The literary pass is refused at the browser boundary, but the production client still runs its independent completion check against the live server, renders both an honest reflection error and the habit offer, and accepting the offer persists the check-in. Detection also records the amount and the user-local day when the entry states them, so the accept logs that amount on that day rather than the goal's target on today; an entry stating neither behaves exactly as before. The literary refusal is deterministic route interception; detection, suggestion persistence, acceptance, and completion are real-wire behavior. The card states those facts before the writer consents rather than only after: the spec asserts the pending offer reads the amount and the day it will log, that the accept button a screen reader announces names them too, and that the persisted goalcompletion row carries that amount on that day rather than the goal's target on today. Once settled, the card names the day the server recorded the accept as logging (the suggestion's persisted logged_on, equal to goalcompletion.local_day), never a day re-derived from the detected day and the live clock: the spec asserts the settled text names that day straight after OK, and again after the entry is reopened the next day and hydrated from the suggestion list alone. The arm where the detected day differs from the logged day (a future or out-of-window detection that fell back to today) is not producible over the real wire, so it is pinned by JournalEntryScreenSuggestions and suggestionFacts instead.

A writer asks for resonance and, when their connected Creek vault recognises a compiled praxis or a recurring eddy in the entry, finds those related pages offered in a collapsed, display-only band beside the journal page. Expanding it shows the page titles, quiet lifecycle or fragment context, and excerpts without turning a pattern into a task. Empty and pre-vault responses leave no band behind. The reflection provider is no longer what blocks this: the lane's default provider now answers a resonance ask with an anchored reading, which is what journal.ask-for-resonance drives. What is still missing is the other half of the response -- a Creek vault fake, connected to the account and seeded with compiled praxis and eddy pages, that answers the reflection with related collections. The activation journey's fake Creek control plane allocates a vault; it does not serve a corpus. The component, hook, and rendered-screen contracts are pinned by the Jest specs beside JournalEntryScreen, and #2408 stays open for this seeded-vault seam.

A writer who has never decided about their corpus asks for resonance on a finished page and, once the reflection has actually landed in the margin, finds beside the page -- never in it -- a quiet note saying reflections can draw on their own earlier writing, what agreeing sends where and how often, and that a yes also sorts what is already written. They can look at the decision, set it aside with Not now, or say Do not ask again; every one of those is one tap, none of them touches the pass, and the answer is kept on the server so it holds across devices and does not return on the next press. On a plain Not now the note returns only after both seven days and three further completed passes; on Do not ask again, or once consent is decided either way, never. The pass count the cooldown runs on never reaches the client. Uncovered as a rendered moment: this journey is about the note appearing beside the page after the pass, and the real-wire lane drives the production client, not the screen. The wire half -- a completed pass opening the offer, and the decline being the server's to remember -- is covered by corpus.decline-the-offer-and-be-left-alone; the rendered half is pinned by the Jest specs beside JournalEntryScreen (placement, one-tap decline, the pass never gated) and by backend/tests/test_resonance_endpoints.py::TestACompletedPassIsCounted for which passes count. The provider seam is no longer what blocks it -- journal.ask-for-resonance now drives a pass that keeps real notes against the default stub provider, and this journey's remaining gap is only the rendered moment, which needs a lane that can mount the screen. #2408 stays open for it rather than being closed by the spec that covered the pass.

A writer who has never decided about their corpus completes a first resonance pass and is offered the decision; they set it aside with Not now and are not asked again on the very next pass; later they say Do not ask again, and a softer Not now afterwards does not undo it. A cold login on a fresh session reads the same standing, because the decision is the server's to remember rather than the device's; a request with no session is refused; and a neighbour's account is still un-asked until its own first pass opens its own offer. The pass that opens the offer is real -- the lane's provider is the stub, so it resolves as a refunded no-notes 200, which is still a completed pass by design -- so the seam this spec pins is the whole of it: the settlement counting the pass, the read the note makes, the verb and shape of both declines, and that the count itself never crosses the wire. Both halves are green on their own -- the note's tests mock the client, the router's tests never see it -- and this is the one place they agree.
A practitioner logs a practice session and finds it in the week's record.
A practitioner who sat without the app logs that sitting afterwards, choosing when it ended and how long it ran, and finds it counted in the week it happened.

A practitioner runs the stage-1 grounding ritual to its end, saves it with a one-line insight, and watches the weekly bar move from 0 of 4 to 1 of 4 in the page they are already looking at. The bar was wired correctly on both sides and still showed the pre-save number: the client incremented optimistically and then refetched, the server counted the new row, and in between GET /practice-sessions/insights advertised max-age=60, so the browser answered the post-save refetch out of its own HTTP cache and put the bar back to zero. No node-lane spec can see that -- node's fetch keeps no HTTP cache, so the request the browser answers for itself is the one the node lane always puts on the wire. This journey runs in the Playwright lane against a real server for exactly that reason, and asserts the server's own week-count alongside the rendered number so a failure separates a lost save from a display that lies about one.

A practitioner who has sat one practice several times walks from the player to that practice's own detail screen -- Practice, its drawer, "Practice details" -- and reads how much they have put into it: total sittings and total time, rendered as hours plus the minutes past 60. The totals are a backend aggregate keyed on an adoption the caller owns, never a client-side sum over a paged session list, and the aggregate widens server-side to every adoption of the same catalog practice that caller owns, so a practice carried from one stage into the next reports one lifetime figure rather than a per-stage slice. The spec logs a zero-length abort alongside two real sittings and asserts it moves neither number, which is the counting rule this endpoint had to settle: the insights rollup skips zero-duration rows, the legacy week-count route does not, and a total cannot honour both. It runs in the Playwright lane because the node lane cannot mount a screen at all (#2324), and because the rollup is read one tap from the player that writes the rows it counts -- the #2654 hazard, which only a browser holding an HTTP cache can see, so the last leg leaves the screen and comes back to force a real re-read.

A practitioner browsing the Practice tab's embedded catalog taps a practice and reads its details in an overlay on that tab rather than on a pushed screen, so the catalog they had narrowed (stage, mode, search, scroll) is still there when they decline: Escape on the web, the Android back button, the corner X or the scrim all close only the overlay, and focus returns to the row that opened it. Choosing the practice from the overlay writes a real adoption and flips straight to the player with it live, never popping a stack that was never pushed. The in-place Practice | Catalog flip the walk crosses in both directions cross-fades (#1952): the surface being left stays mounted, out of reach of touch and assistive tech, for one motion.threshold and then unmounts, which the spec checks under the browser's own animation driver; the fade's timing, reduced-motion swap and fail-open floor are pinned in Jest. The details come from the real GET /practices/{practice_id} and the choice from the real POST /user-practices/, which the Jest suite mocks and the node lane cannot mount a screen to reach. The overlay is not a route, so the browser's back button leaves the tab rather than closing it -- an accepted limitation the spec deliberately does not assert on.

A practitioner starts a meditation timer from the Practice screen and hears the session open, pass its halfway mark, and close, then logs the sitting. Uncovered, for two reasons rather than the usual one. The first is the familiar one: this lane runs on the node environment with node_modules untransformed and cannot mount a screen at all (#2324). The second is specific and is the reason this entry exists at all -- audibility is not assertable anywhere in this repository. There is no frontend/ios and no frontend/android, so nothing here runs on a device, and the two surviving acceptance criteria of #1419 ("a session audibly strikes start/half/end on device" and "bowl/chime/gong are three distinguishable sounds") are owner sign-off items. What ships in their place are substitutes, and they are named as substitutes: a peak-amplitude assertion on the rendered PCM, and a Goertzel dominant-frequency separation between all six timbres, in bellSynth.test.ts. Those prove the bytes are not silence and not the same bell twice; they do not prove a human in a room hears a bell. The bug this journey was written against is exactly the gap between those two claims -- six 0-byte mp3s resolved to valid modules, constructed players without throwing, and played nothing, so the failure was invisible to the user and to the logs alike, and the component test that was meant to guard it asserted only that a player had been constructed.
A practitioner submits a custom practice and adopts it as one they can actually do.

A reader opens a stage's content, reads a piece, and marks it read so progress moves. Course opens on the last Frequency marked read; the date/server current stage applies only before any reading or when that Frequency is locked after a reset. Explicit route parameters keep precedence. The cold start's bounded wait is pinned in-process by src/features/Course/__tests__/CourseScreenColdStart.test.tsx over the same GET /stages request.

A new reader opens Course on ordered Start Here resources, reads actual served Markdown, marks resources through the reader, reloads to retain confirmed marks, and uses Read next through every resource into an unlocked chapter. Chromium covers phone and desktop with normal and targeted doubled rendered text; this is not native OS text-scale certification. A reader opens the served Energy Scaffolding resource from the Course drawer, then uses its separate action to open the existing Habits onboarding on both cold and mounted Habits tabs. The browser explicitly exits the existing discard confirmation, verifies a disabled Habits ring removes the Course action, and holds an unchanged real server-disabled preference response during cold hydration to prove the action cannot bypass an unconfirmed ring. It opens onboarding only; it does not claim to create or reorder habits. Phone and desktop inspect targeted doubled resource drawer/action text above the footer fade.

Two fresh accounts share a null program anchor. The outgoing account reads Course Start Here, then a controlled 401 on its next Frequency read (and on /auth/refresh) raises the re-auth sheet over the still-mounted Course, where the incoming account signs in; a document witness proves the running app never reloaded. Without a remount, Start Here shows the incoming account's own resources and server-confirmed read mark, Read next is re-asked for that account rather than keeping the outgoing answer, and the confirmed resource opens from the keyboard in the real reader as already read. Chromium covers phone and desktop at normal and targeted doubled rendered text (not native OS text-scale certification) with clipping checks. Held outgoing Start Here and Read next answers, A-to-B-to-A, the credential gap, a failed incoming load with retry, explicit Frequency routes, and same-session renewal are covered by the mounted CourseScreen jest suite, not by this browser spec.

On bare /course entry the stage list loads while a controlled 503 fails one Start Here read: GET /course/site-resources at normal text, GET /course/start-here/progress at doubled text, so each read fails at both phone and desktop widths. The Course does not fall back to its full-screen error: unknown progress opens Start Here (never the saved Frequency, which only finished progress can reach), which says the read failed, hides any progress count and offers a 44px 'Try again'. The stage pills still open a healthy stage-1 chapter in the real reader, and the drawer still lists the stages with its own Start Here retry. Once the read can succeed, Try again is reached with Tab (its focus ring inspected) and pressed with Enter; Start Here then shows the server-confirmed resources in order with the pre-marked first resource read, the right 'N of M read' count, and a re-asked, resource-first Read next past the confirmed resource, while the selection stays on Start Here. Chromium covers 390px and 1280px at normal and targeted doubled rendered text (not native OS text-scale certification) with clipping checks. A retry that fails again, a failed Read next lookup, explicit Frequency routes and the owner/generation protections are pinned by the mounted CourseScreen jest suites (CourseScreenStartHereFailure, CourseScreenAccountSwitch), not by this browser spec.

At desktop and phone widths, a reader marks a Blue chapter read while the program calendar is on Orange, then reloads Course without route parameters and finds Blue selected. The browser uses the real reader scroll and mark-read action, GET /ui-flags, and GET /stages without response stubs.

A reader taps Read next in the Course header and lands on the next page they have not read. While any Start Here resource is unread that is the lowest-order one, opened in the resource reader, whose body is served; marking it read moves the target to the next resource, and once Start Here is read through the target is the earliest unlocked chapter they have not read, across every open stage: lowest stage first, then release order. Marking chapter 1 read moves the target to chapter 2, whose reader body is served; once a stage is read through the target crosses into the next open stage, and with nothing open left unread the button reads All caught up. The covering spec drives the real client against a live server after moving only the program anchor; the tap itself -- setParams into the route-param path useReaderRestore already opens, a resource target opening the resource reader, and the re-fetch after either mark-read -- is pinned in-process by src/features/Course/__tests__/CourseScreenReadNext.test.tsx.

A reader in a desktop browser opens a chapter, chooses Write a note on a passage, selects a passage by keyboard, double-click, and pointer drag, confirms Write a note, lands in JournalEntry with the passage prefilled as a blockquote, and waits for the entry to save. The covering Playwright spec boots the real Expo web app and FastAPI app over loopback against an alembic-built throwaway Postgres database; it exists because the Node API lane cannot exercise native textarea selection or browser accessibility semantics.

A reader finishes a chapter, marks it read, and taps Reflect in Journal. The writing surface opens already titled for the stage and the chapter, the reflection saves, and the way out is the way in: Back to reading returns them to that same chapter instead of leaving them on the Journal shelf to find the Course tab by hand. Sibling to course.write-note-on-passage, which drives the reader's other hand-off; this one is the reflection, which closes the reader behind it and so returns to the chapter rather than to a scroll position. It runs in the browser lane because the whole journey is screen-to-screen navigation -- the returnTo that makes the exit exist never crosses the wire, so no amount of API driving could see whether it is there. Verified to be a live gate rather than a passing formality: with the returnTo removed from handleReflect the spec fails on the absent Back to reading control.

A user whose first page of habits is full opens Habits in a desktop browser and, after a viewport flip to a phone profile, in one column. The covering Playwright spec signs up through the UI, seeds ten habits over POST /habits/ with a token from POST /auth/login, and then measures laid-out DOM: the grid's box ends at or above the top of both the pagination bar and the Energy Scaffolding CTA, and every tile lies inside the grid's box -- the first before any scrolling, the last after scrolling the grid to its end. It exists because the Jest lanes cannot answer a layout question at all: this project runs the node environment under the React Native preset, so onLayout never fires and every box is zero, which is why issue #2658's report of a grid "clipped beneath fixed controls" survived a green suite. Nothing here asserts that a full page fits without scrolling; the same spec measured 147px of overflow at 1280x720 and 129px at 390x844, and records those numbers on every run instead of claiming a fit the app does not hold.

A traveller opens the Map after the calendar has moved them into a new stage, and the server agrees they moved. Advance is not an action a person takes: the calendar over the ratified 21x8+42x2 schedule decides what is offered, and reading the Map records that the person entered it. There is deliberately no tap affordance -- a manual advance contradicts the earned, server-derived progression model -- so the covering spec moves the program anchor in the lane's own database and then reads, never posts. The three reads below are the whole of what the Map asks for: GET /stages/{stage_number}/progress is served but unreachable, and naming it here described a seam the app has no half of. Unlocking alone would prove nothing, because access is the union of the calendar and the record; so the spec asserts the record itself -- current_stage, completed_stages, stage_started_at -- moved when the Map was read, stayed put when the anchor moved without a read, and re-recorded nothing on a second read inside the same window.

A traveller opens the Map drawer and reads one framing sentence between the journey read and the ten stage rows: 'The Map is a wheel, not a ladder: its ten stages revisit different capacities, never ranking you or the stages.' It appears exactly once, describes only the rendered stage-and-capacity rows, and introduces no invented fullness, altitude or person-ranking vocabulary. The same real-browser walk first visits the successful-empty Journal and Habits surfaces and filters the Practice catalog to its three empty sections, proving each names the gain of filling it. At 390x844, 1280x800 and effective 200% browser zoom it asserts horizontal containment, journey-lead-row order and reachable actions, and saves every product surface for visual inspection with each Practice section captured separately; the enlarged drawer labels wrap instead of clipping.

A traveller opens the current stage on the Map and takes its strongest action, Continue, directly into that stage's Course chapter. The stage modal offers Course exactly once through that primary action; Practice and Journal occupy the two secondary slots, so no destination is duplicated. The component journey separately pins the stage-number route parameter and the close-before-navigation/double-tap guard, while this real-browser journey proves the rendered accessibility name, action hierarchy, modal dismissal, tab hand-off, and selected Course cover together.

Someone reads the Map at any viewport and every stage annotation stays legible: the Aspect word, a locked stage's padlock and "Opens ..." estimate, and a finished stage's check badge each stay off the wave's painted stroke, off each other and on screen, inside their own stage's cell and band, and a window too short for the table scrolls it rather than painting one stage onto the next (#2657); the lens's own caption -- the YOU ARE HERE chip, the stage title and subtitle -- stays on the glass, inside the rim and clear of the pill's rounded ends, so a caption set larger must grow the pill (#2960). Every grid size is a ramp step (#2960): stage copy that fits no step wraps at the 13px caption floor instead of shrinking, and each stage's left and center cells share one row that never shrinks below the taller cell's content, so a wrapped line or a long unlock estimate grows its own stage rather than spilling into the stage stacked with it; the right label is inset inside its cell, which is left unpadded so the columns keep the 2/2/1 flex split the wave is drawn to. Every line of every right-column aspect label reads whole -- never cut to an ellipsis -- and inside its own band: a label too wide for its cell by the glyph estimate falls back to its hyphenated lines (Aware- / ness on every standard phone from 320 to 414 wide, Under- / standing, Yes-And- / Ness), and no label line is capped with numberOfLines, so a line that runs wider than the estimate on any serif face wraps rather than truncating; a fifth test sweeps this rule across every phone width from 320 to 390 in 5px steps. At a desktop window the completed Map scrolls by no more than Begin again's button, so the whole table and Begin again's words read without scrolling; the top stage's cell takes no extra height for the lens when it is current, since the lens then overhangs only stage 9's UNITY watermark. The covering spec measures three states -- fresh (stage 1, stages 2-10 locked), partial (stage 5, stages 1-4 finished, second cycle so the cycle caption shows) and completed (stage 10 finished, Begin again showing) -- at 1280x720 and 390x844, plus a 1280x560 window for fresh and completed, each in one settled frame: two animation frames, then the text census and a sample of every wave path every 2px of arc (getPointAtLength through getScreenCTM) in the same evaluate. The current stage moves the only way it can, through tests.e2e.program_anchor (90 and 240 days back); per-stage completion has no writer at all, so the spec lets GET /stages and GET /stages/program-calendar reach the lane's server and rewrites only progress and cycle_number on the response -- nothing on the Map is stubbed. Before any rule runs it proves it measured something: a wave with length, and exactly as many unlock lines, padlocks in each column and badges as the state has locked and finished stages. The rules are pure functions in frontend/e2e/mapGeometry.ts pinned by src/design/__tests__/mapGeometry.test.ts. Each measure waits for its state to be established -- the calendar's stage in the journey read and under the lens's YOU ARE HERE chip, the cycle caption, Begin again -- and asserts those markers in the measured frame. A fourth test drags the lens with real touches (Input.dispatchTouchEvent in a touch context at 390x664, where the fresh Map scrolls): the lens moves and the Map's scroller stays put, while the same gesture on the table's text does scroll it. The magnifier pill and the EMPTINESS / UNITY watermark the converging wave rises through by design are the only intended covers. Screenshots and the measured frame land in e2e/artifacts/map-legibility/ for review; there is no pixel baseline.

Someone turns a depth ring on or off and the app they come back to is the one they chose: Habits, Practice and Course each add or remove their primary destination; Sangha adds or removes the Digital Sangha door in Settings (SanghaSection.tsx), and its switch is offered only in a build with EXPO_PUBLIC_SANGHA_INVITE_URL configured, because a switch with nothing to close would be a false choice. The live-wire spec proves enable_sangha round-trips independently; the in-process pairing of each switch with its destination is pinned by src/features/Settings/__tests__/depthSwitchesHaveEffect.test.tsx.

A writer who declines every optional depth keeps a whole journal and is never invited back into a ring they turned off (#3073). On a fresh account (no corpus consent, no vault of their own, not the deployment vault's owner) Habits, Practices and Course are switched off through the real Settings switches and Sangha over PATCH /depth-preferences (its switch ships only in a build with a Sangha invite URL), and the stored state is read back. The drawer then lists no Habits, Practice or Course destination. The writer writes a page and runs a timed writing session to its end -- the finished-session note is the offer that used to show with habits off. The spec waits for the note's withheld marker, which renders only once the offer has read its stored answer and found both depths declined, and only then asserts no keep-as-habit or keep-as-practice offer, so the absence cannot be read during the offer's loading window. The page is found by search, reopened, exported (both export routes, and the Export screen renders) and deleted, and GET /invitations answers [] on the all-off path. Return cards, invitation cards, the contraction reflection and the link-a-habit pointer cannot appear on a fresh account, so they are pinned below rather than asserted absent here. Finally the lane's fake language-model provider and fake Creek vault counters are unchanged, so nothing left the box. The server-side gates are pinned in backend/tests: routers/test_invitations.py (a declined ring's pending invitations are hidden and return on re-enable, a course-off listing never reads the vault wheel, all-off generates nothing), services/test_invitations_service.py, routers/test_contraction_reflection.py (habits off -> contraction null) and routers/test_journal_journal_only.py (a fresh account's save at every tier and with every ring off builds no real vault client, calls no provider and opens no outbound request). Jest pins each client gate: DepthGate.test.tsx, JournalShelfScreen.test.tsx (Return hidden with habits off), InvitationStack.test.tsx (a declined ring's cards drop live, with no remount), WritingSessionOffer.test.tsx (only the kept depths' accepts beside the decline; nothing with both off), JournalEntryScreenTimer.test.tsx and JournalEntryScreenContraction.test.tsx. The journal-only browser spec also delays a genuine old GET response until after a real keyboard PATCH confirms a decline, then verifies the switch stays declined, the server GET agrees, and reload preserves it, at 390 and 1280 pixels with normal and 200% text (#3279). Delayed-promise Jest regressions cover independent concurrent invitation declines, same-account token refresh, account changes, reset and per-field preference read/write ordering; those are not claimed as browser account-switch or physical-device verification.

A person who HAS connected a vault chooses a document from their device and seeds it there -- since #3017 the picker is offered only to an account the server does not say has nothing attached, so an account with no vault is shown where its corpus lives first (corpus.bring-in-your-writing-needs-a-vault-first); the import forwards to the vault rather than persisting locally, so authentication is the only table it crosses. One route serves every account -- POST /corpus/import decides per account -- and this entry is the vault half of that decision; the no-vault half, answered vault_required with nothing stored (#3016), is corpus.import-without-a-vault. The lane now has a vault to reach: a loopback process answering Creek's published GET /v1/capabilities and POST /v1/uploads, reached through adepthood's own production CREEK_VAULT_URL and bound to one pre-provisioned account by CREEK_VAULT_OWNER_USER_ID. That binding is what closed the last blocker -- the variable is read from the server's environment and so names an id fixed before any account exists, which globalSetup settles by signing that account up as the lane's first request and refusing the whole run if the id it gets back is not the one already named. The deployment-wide value is also the only one that may name loopback: a user-supplied vault URL is refused unless it names a globally routable destination, which is why the connect-your-own path cannot serve this. The spec proves the seam end to end -- accepted with a ref, a re-send reported as one fragment edited in place rather than a second, and an Intimate document withheld before the vault is contacted at all, asserted against the vault's own record of what arrived.

A person with a vault seeds a document and the vault keeps it, but its reply is lost on the way back -- a timeout, a dropped connection, or a 2xx adepthood cannot read. POST /corpus/import answers 202 degraded, and since #3052 both the server's message and the row beneath the document say the upload could not be confirmed and that sending the same file again updates it in place, never that nothing was stored. Since #3239 the same holds when it is the app's own request that loses its answer -- a client-side timeout, a dropped connection, a 5xx, or a reply the app cannot read settles as unconfirmed rather than failed -- and the run summary counts these apart from the documents that didn't go over; only a 4xx refusal keeps "nothing was stored", and a device the platform reports offline is never sent and says so. Uncovered because the lane's fake vault has no mode that commits an upload and then spoils its reply; pinned meanwhile by test_document_upload_to_a_vault.py (a committing-then-losing transport driven through the real HTTP adapter) and seedCopy.test.ts.

Someone the server finds no vault for brings in a document they wrote elsewhere. A corpus lives in a vault (owner ruling on #3015), so since #3016 the answer is vault_required and nothing else happens: the document is not read, consent is not consulted, no provider is called and nothing is stored -- destination corpus, stored false, fragment_id null, vault fields null. The spec proves the document was never looked at by sending each thing the retired local import used to answer differently -- a .md with no consent, a .pdf, the same .md after turning the switch for documents on, an Intimate document, and a neighbour who agreed to nothing -- and getting the same answer every time. It still crosses PUT /corpus/consent/{source} on purpose: flipping the switch is how it proves the switch now lets nothing in.

Someone brings in a batch and leaves the screen before it has all gone over. The screen asks first rather than silently discarding the run, and confirming genuinely stops it: the document already in flight finishes wherever it lands, and everything still queued is never sent. The point of the journey is the seam, not the prompt -- what has to be proved is that the account's vault afterwards holds exactly the documents that had settled on screen (an account with no vault keeps nothing at all since #3016, each item settling as vault_required, so only a vault account has anything to read back), because the defect this closes was a run that kept uploading in the background while the person saw an empty screen. Covered at the hook and screen level by Jest (useSeedRun, useSeedLeaveGuard, SeedCorpusScreen), which can only assert that the client stopped calling the route; uncovered here because no spec yet reads the corpus back to confirm the server agrees.

A corpus lives in a vault (owner ruling on #3015), and since #3016 the server keeps nothing a vault-less account sends, so 'Bring in your writing' waits for a place to keep what comes in (#3017). In Settings the Your corpus group now leads with Where your writing lives; for an account GET /vault/connection says has nothing attached, the seed row keeps its name and icon but says where that place is set up, and opens Where your writing lives rather than the picker. Unknown -- a read still out, a read that failed, or a provider-managed vault answered with no address -- is never read as none and keeps the picker, with the server's vault_required as the backstop. The spec drives this unstubbed on a fresh lane account, which has no vault of its own and is not the deployment binding's owner. The Journal band (CTA 'Give your writing a place to live'), the Journal drawer's Everything you've written door and the seeding screen's own invitation take the same rule and are pinned in their component suites (VoiceReadinessBand, JournalEntryScreenDrawer, JournalShelfScreenDrawer, SeedCorpusScreen). Known gap: the deployment binding's single owner has no connection row and so is shown the same invitation although their imports land.

Someone takes a copy of everything they have written: they open Export my data, the app downloads the JSON archive and the Markdown journal, saves both to the device and offers them to the share sheet. The archive carries their own entries as prose, never another account's, and never the ciphertext the column holds. Beta feedback reports (the feedbackreport table) travel in the same archive under feedback_reports; that half is proven at the seam by feedback.admin-triage-inbox.

Someone saves their own OpenAI or Anthropic key on the device, then uses a model-powered feature. The production app sends the key over HTTPS to Adepthood in the X-LLM-API-Key header, and Adepthood forwards it over HTTPS to the selected provider for that request without persisting, logging, or returning it. Both Settings surfaces disclose those two service boundaries before the key is used. The copy and wire contract are pinned together by src/features/Settings/__tests__/byokDisclosure.test.ts and the rendered-screen specs beside it. The real-wire lane cannot cover the whole journey because it neither mounts SecureStore-backed Settings screens nor sends a live credential to an external model provider; doing so would turn a test fixture into a production secret and a billable third-party call. Page reading is the exception since ADR 0009 phase (a)'s second half (#3067): with a key, the device sends the key and the page straight to that key's vendor, Adepthood sees only a content-free admission request and declares no key header on its page-read route, and both Settings surfaces and the privacy policy say so in the owner's 2026-10-14 wording (#3260). That path is journal.page-read-with-own-key-goes-device-to-vendor.

Someone who saved their own model key on this device removes it from Settings. The press opens a rendered confirmation (not Alert.alert, which react-native-web ships as an empty method and which left the key irremovable on web, #2928); Cancel keeps the key and Remove clears it, and it is still gone after a reload. Removal itself is device-local and calls no route, so the journey proves what removal is for, on both ways the client picks a key, reached from the entry's own API-key shortcut in the same browser session. The resonance pass passes its disclosed payer explicitly: after removal it is disclosed as the shared allowance, leaves without the X-LLM-API-Key header, and raises monthly_messages_used by one, which catches a build that hid the card while the key stayed in context. The margin-note essay passes no key and so reads the session getter ApiKeyContext registers: opened after removal and before any reload, it too leaves without the header, which catches a build whose in-memory getter kept returning the removed key (the explicit-key pass cannot, since it never consults the getter). Controls made while the key is stored carry the header -- the pass itself, and the completion check the refused pass runs through the getter -- so the header's later absence is observed rather than assumed. The controls are answered in the browser and never reach a server, and the spec asserts the lane fake provider's shared attempt counters are unchanged at its end, because later specs require them to start at zero.

Someone opens API-key Settings and sees Adepthood's own model as a disabled coming-soon control, without a present-tense promise that their writing already stays on Adepthood infrastructure. Even if an older build left the local-model preference switched on in device storage, this unavailable option renders off, keeps the key controls usable, and cannot suppress the BYOK header on the person's next model request. Uncovered because the browser lane cannot yet seed that legacy device preference while mounting this Settings screen and then observe the request wire in one journey; the screen and context regressions pin the guard until that lane exists.

Someone opens the corpus-consent screen, finds every kind of material off and un-asked, turns their journal on, and later turns it back off -- which deletes the copies it collected and leaves a dated refusal on the record rather than an open question. Turning it on now reaches backwards as well: the entries already in their journal are sorted on the same terms as a new one, bounded so the request they are waiting on stays finite. The spec covers the switch and the deletion; what it cannot yet observe is the reach, because the lane has no classification provider, so a backfilled entry settles as unclassified and writes no fragment for a spec to see. A provider that refuses to bill now ends that reach rather than consuming the queue, and never costs the person the permission they just gave -- the switch still answers granted and the entries it did not get to keep their place. The backend pins it at backend/tests/test_corpus_consent_api.py.

The Settings hub keeps its inline sorting switches. Pushing What reflections draw on while the genuine consent GET is held reuses the same read; a real confirmed PUT grant appears in the detail and the retained hub. The hub withdrawal still asks, cancellation writes nothing, confirmation is retained after reload. Phone and desktop normal and targeted doubled rendered Settings text keep copy contained, keyboard grant reachable and withdrawal targets44px. This browser proof does not certify native text scaling, corpus classification providers or live vendor retention.

Someone who has just given their corpus a vault is told, on the vault screen, that creating one does not turn sorting on and that the yes is a switch under Your corpus in Settings. On the hub, that group now carries the sorting switches themselves -- one per kind of material the server names, under a one-line lead that says what sorting is for, what it sends and that Intimate is never sent -- between Bring in your writing and the What reflections draw on row that holds the full account. The switches are the same component the sub-screen mounts (CorpusConsentRows), so turning a source on records the decision over PUT /corpus/consent/{source} and shows only the state the server reported back, and turning one off asks first, naming the deletion, before anything is withdrawn. Uncovered because the browser lane presses the switches only on the sub-screen (corpus.decide-what-may-be-sorted); the hub mount is pinned by SettingsHubScreen.test.tsx (the switches' place in the group, the lead's three facts, the grant and the revoke question) and the vault copy by vaultCopy.test.ts.

Someone ends their account from inside the app: they read what goes and what stays, retype their own address to confirm, and the server erases them and hands back a receipt. The receipt's vault half is account-scoped rather than deployment-scoped. This lane does have a deployment-wide vault for seed.upload-document, but globalSetup binds that single corpus to one pre-provisioned owner; the later account created by this journey has no per-user connection and must therefore receive `configured: false` with no-vault guidance, never a claim on the other person's vault. Backend API regressions separately pin manual owner, per-user connection, unconfigured, and provisioned teardown receipts. Erasure takes the account's beta feedback reports (feedbackreport) with it; that half is proven at the seam by feedback.admin-triage-inbox, where the operator can no longer open or list them.

At phone and desktop sizes, an authenticated Habits read fails with a malformed response or server error containing private canaries. The existing error card and Retry remain reachable; every captured console argument omits private prose, request IDs and validation issue text. Clearing the fault and retrying reads a real persisted habit through the authenticated API and restores the Habits surface. Crash-envelope minimization is separately tested at the production transport boundary; this journey does not claim the renderer crash flow.

A feature screen throws while a journal entry is on screen; the boundary shows the recovery card, "Try again" remounts the subtree, and the crash report that leaves the device carries none of what was written. Still uncovered because the e2e lane cannot mount a screen at all: it runs on the node environment with node_modules untransformed, so importing the boundary dies on @react-navigation/native's ESM and react-native's Flow syntax, and the lane's own guard pins the moduleNameMapper to the @/ alias so the React Native preset cannot be added to a spec. Observing the outgoing crash envelope is banned in this lane by the same guard. Covering it needs a second, rendering lane, not another spec here.

The server hits an unhandled exception while the journal shelf is loading; the app says something went wrong on our end and offers the server's request id as a reference, instead of telling the user to check their wifi. Each side is pinned separately: backend/tests/middleware/test_unhandled_exception_cors.py drives the real app and asserts the 500 leaves it carrying Access-Control-Allow-Origin, and src/api/__tests__/serverErrorIsNotOffline.test.ts asserts the client keeps the sanitised envelope's code and request id while a failure that produced no response at all reads as the server being unreachable. That last arm changed with #2661: a request a browser blocks on CORS and a request that reaches nothing are the same bare TypeError to JavaScript -- measured in Chromium, identical message, properties, and resource-timing entry -- so the copy no longer diagnoses the device, and the "you appear to be offline" claim is raised only behind the client's own connectivity signal. Both arms are pinned in src/api/__tests__/corsRejectionIsNotOffline.test.ts. Uncovered here because the real-wire lane has no way to make the live server 500 — every reachable failure is a deliberate 4xx or 503, and adding a fault-injection route to the production app to manufacture one would be worse than the gap.

A device that already holds one account's session is signed into by a second account without an explicit logout -- through the password-reset flow, or any path that reaches the login screen with a live cache on disk. The incoming user must see none of the previous user's habits, none of their check-in queue replayed under the new token, and none of their BYOK key on the resonance header. Uncovered because the leak is a row on the device rather than a row on the server: this lane drives HTTP against a live backend from Node, with no app process and therefore no AsyncStorage or SecureStore to seed, dirty, or read back, so a spec written against the wire could only assert that the backend scopes reads to its caller -- which it already did throughout, and which was never the failing half. Held meanwhile by src/context/__tests__/AccountSwitchWipe.integration.test.tsx, which drives the real AuthProvider and the real habitStorage against the in-memory AsyncStorage mock, plus the per-account namespacing tests in src/storage/__tests__/. The cold start behind that door is held by src/context/__tests__/ResumedSessionScope.integration.test.tsx, which pins the namespace a resumed session reads to the subject of the token it resumed rather than to a separately persisted stamp the two non-atomic sign-in writes can leave disagreeing. What that meanwhile-guard holds now includes the device-cached timezone: the switch drops the outgoing account's zone, and drops it before the incoming account's is written to the same unscoped device key, so a failed write cannot leave the previous account's calendar driving the next one's day boundary.

A writer asks for resonance while the balance behind the key that pays for it is spent. What they got was "the AI provider is having trouble connecting, give it a moment and tap retry" -- a transient story for a permanent, billing-level refusal, so the retry button they were pointed at could never work and the real cause reached nobody. The journey now ends in copy that names the condition and the one action that clears it, with no retry affordance and nothing charged. The browser spec presses "Get Resonance" against the real server with the caller's own key (402), and neither it nor the counterweight raises the typed error: the lane points the production SDK clients at a loopback fake through their own OPENAI_BASE_URL / ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL, so openai.RateLimitError is built by the SDK out of the provider's real refusal body, which is the classification the bug turned on. The counterweight -- a genuine rate limit, same provider and same 429 with a different code -- keeps its transient copy and its retry. Since ADR 0009 phase (a) (#3067) the server's own key never pays for a writer's page, so the former 503 half (the server's own spent balance) is replaced: with the server's LLM_API_KEY and the retired provider-probe marker both still armed, a keyless page reaches no provider at all and costs the writer nothing; an intimate page carrying the same marker likewise reaches none. walletaudit is read out of band to show who paid. Each side is still pinned separately: backend/tests/services/test_botmason_credit_exhausted.py drives both SDKs through a mock transport so each builds its own typed error from the provider's real body, backend/tests/security/test_byok_only_cloud.py proves zero cloud calls without the writer's key, and src/api/__tests__/errorMessages.test.ts asserts neither code inherits the transient copy.

Someone who made their own practice tag renames it, and later deletes it, from the recipe editor's tag library. The library could list and create and stopped there, so both routes were served, typed, and unreachable from any screen. The journey is the seam: that a rename reaches the row the client named and survives the next list rather than living in local state, that the slug a recipe step copied by value is untouched by it, that a shared tag refuses both mutations from the server rather than from what the client chose to render, and that deleting a personal tag leaves the shared library whole.

Someone writing a journal page -- including a Course reader writing a reflection, which is an ordinary page opened with a prefilled title -- taps the camera in the entry's top-right row (beside the key and the close X), photographs a page or screenshot of their response -- handwritten, typed, printed, or a screenshot of a message thread, which transcribes as sender-labelled lines -- and the transcription is appended into the entry they already had open rather than being filed as a second one. Overlapping screenshots of one thread merge without repeating the overlap: where two adjacent pages repeat lines at their seam (a cropped line at either edge included), the merged transcript carries them once, a quiet per-page notice counts the repeated lines by page position, and a "Keep them" action restores both copies for that seam; each page's stored text is never altered, a short or single coincidental repeat is never dropped, lines whose numbers, times, symbols or emoji differ never count as repeats, and a seam beside a hand-edited page is left whole so the writer's correction always reaches the entry (#2929). The seam is what makes that a single entry: the capture route hands the merged transcript back through an in-memory store and the open page's own create-then-update writer persists it, so the title and save context the writer arrived with survive and one POST /journal/ covers the whole journey. The outcome also includes a page read the writer cannot retry past -- no key of their own (key_required) or a spent balance on it (credit_exhausted) -- which shows the terminal copy and hand-typed-entry offramp and keeps Save disabled (#2849; the former model_lacks_vision outcome is retired, since a page read with a key now always asks the vendor for a vision model, #3067); and an image with no text, or a read the model declines, which the server answers with an uncharged 422 no_text_found / transcription_refused that the page offers to Retake or Remove, never as its text (#2851). Uncovered because neither lane can drive the capture: the route auto-launches the device photo picker on mount, which the node lane cannot even mount (#2324) and which no browser spec has ever driven through a file chooser, and the transcription itself is a charged vision call that needs the lane's LLM stub wired through it.

A writer who has saved their own OpenAI or Anthropic key photographs a page. The page and the key go from their device straight to that key's vendor (ADR 0009 phase (a), #3067): the app first asks Adepthood's content-free POST /journal/transcribe-page/direct-admission (its body is the page's declared tier and nothing else: no key, no page; 204, or 403 tier_refused for any tier but personal or public (#3059), or 503 ai_suspended while an operator has switched external AI off, and the page is then not sent; an unreachable admission also stops it), then calls https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages (with anthropic-dangerous-direct-browser-access, which Anthropic requires before it answers a browser) or https://api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions with the same prompt and token budget the server used and that vendor's registry default model (gpt-4o-mini or claude-sonnet-5; the operator's LLM_MODEL does not govern a device-direct read), and judges the reply by the same rules, so an empty read or a refusal is no_text_found / transcription_refused and never the page's text; a kept read is appended into the open entry exactly as on the server path. A spent vendor balance, a vendor rate limit, a bad key, a timeout and a dropped connection keep the kinds and copy the server path had. Without a key, a production build refuses key_required on the device and sends the page nowhere (only a development build still reaches its local server's stub seam). The server's page-read route declares no key header and runs its payer gate before decoding a body; a key sent to it anyway by a stale client is never read, forwarded or logged, and the request is refused llm_key_required. Uncovered because no lane can drive it: the capture route auto-launches the device photo picker (journal.photograph-a-page-into-the-open-entry), and a covering spec would need a live vendor credential and a billable third-party call, or a vendor fake the enforced CSP's connect-src admits. Pinned meanwhile by src/api/__tests__/transcribePage.test.ts and byokDirect.test.ts (request shape, error taxonomy, privacy, CSP origins), src/api/__tests__/transcriptionContract.test.ts and backend/tests/test_transcription_client_contract.py (one shared fixture: prompt and token budget captured off the server's own wire request, the registry default models, and the classifier's verdicts over every refusal opener and cue), and backend/tests/security/test_byok_only_cloud.py (the admission carries only a tier and honours the suspension; a key sent to the page route is never forwarded or logged).

A writer photographing a page chooses its tier before Transcribe. Choosing intimate turns transcription off in place (#1882): Transcribe is disabled, a calm gate says intimate writing is never handed to an outside AI and offers 'Type it instead' (a fresh typed entry pre-set to intimate) or 'Keep as Personal', and no read is ever started. Behind that gate the server now learns the tier too (#3059 AC15): every page read declares the classification the writer chose, on both paths -- the server-relayed POST /journal/transcribe-page and the device-direct admission POST /journal/transcribe-page/direct-admission -- and any tier but personal or public (intimate, an unknown tier, the empty string, a wrong-case spelling) is refused 403 tier_refused before the incident switch, the vault boundary, the payer gate, the slot, the wallet, the usage log or any dial; a request with no tier is refused by the schema. In append mode -- the camera on a page already being written (journal.photograph-a-page-into-the-open-entry) -- the entry hands its own tier to the capture with the hand-off token (appendTier) as the tier as it stands when the camera is pressed, and that tier is a floor: the capture starts there, may narrow toward intimate but never widen, and offers no 'Keep as Personal' below it; an Intimate entry therefore opens the capture on the gate and reads nothing ('Type it instead' returns to the page), and a missing or unrecognised tier fails closed to intimate. The client maps tier_refused to the same gate copy, as a terminal failure: no Retry, no Retake, no further page of the run started, Save disabled and the hand-typed-entry offramp shown. Uncovered because neither lane can drive the capture (journal.photograph-a-page-into-the-open-entry: the route auto-launches the device photo picker). Pinned meanwhile by backend/tests/security/test_transcription_tier_refusal.py (each refusal with a delegating spy on every seam and a personal/public counterweight that watches the same spies fire), src/api/__tests__/transcribePage.test.ts, and the Jest suites JournalPhotographScreen (including append mode from intimate, personal, public, missing and unrecognised tiers), JournalEntryScreenPhotograph (the hand-off carries the entry's tier), useTranscriptionRun and transcriptionRun.

A writer uses the same journal entry at 390x844, the 600px two-column boundary, and 1280x720, writing and then reading. Live browser boxes, each viewport read in one settled frame, prove every control keeps one home (#3002, #3004). While writing, the icon-only camera sits in the entry's top-right exit row directly left of the close X (same line, at least a 44px target, its full phrase only as the accessible name, and key, camera, X ahead of the title in DOM order), with no Edit beside it; neither the exit row nor the page scrolls sideways; the formatting toolbar sits below the exit row and above the body, then the save footer and Finish alone and centred follow the body input (#3250). Actual Tab navigation passes from the title through Bold, Italic and Underline to the body; these controls and Finish also follow that DOM order. After the real autosave creates the entry and the writer pauses, Get Resonance is measured inside and centred on the wide marginalia column, its longest preflight state is held and measured within that fixed column, and at 600px and on the phone it is still the one Get Resonance on the page, inside the margin (stacked under the page on the phone) and in the page flow, never floating. Finishing turns the page to reading: at 390 and 1280 an icon-only Edit (accessible name 'Edit this entry') sits in the exit row directly left of the X on one line, at least 44px, with no camera and no Edit in the reading row; Promote sits below the save hint; resonance stays in the margin; nothing scrolls sideways. The journey then makes a real curriculum reflection due, opens it through the shelf invitation, writes a line so Finish appears, and at 600, 390 and 375px measures the reflection-only Sources as an icon in the exit row -- key, Sources, camera, X ahead of the title -- all on one line without sideways scroll, with neither Sources nor the camera on the rail and Finish still centred under the page, covering the widest writing row rather than inferring its geometry from component props.

A writer gives a page a title too long for one line and sees every line of it, at every width (#3325). The title is a growing field sized to its text, so a wrapped title belongs to the page flow, never to an inner scroll. The real browser lays the title's value out in a twin with the field's computed face, width and inset and proves every line box sits inside the field's visible padding box, nothing is left to scroll (scrollHeight within clientHeight, scrollTop 0), the field never runs under the hairline below it, and it holds no more than its lines and inset. The journey types the original report's title ('A page with steady controls') at 1280x720 and narrows to 390x844, where it now wraps to two visible lines instead of hiding the second; types a long title key by key at 390; widens to 1280 and sees the spare lines given back; edits the title in place at 390 and presses Enter to land in the body with the edited value kept; then closes, lets the real POST /journal/ save it, reopens it from the shelf and measures the loaded title at 390 and 1280. A second run at 200% browser zoom on a phone (195x422 CSS px at device scale 2) types and then sets a long title and measures it the same way. Jest pins the width-change and font-settlement re-measures in useGrowingFieldHeight and the twin measurement in webFieldMeasure.

The Prompts inline history uses GET /prompts/history to retain answered questions with their original responses, newest first. This API journey proves joined question/response data and server-side limit/offset paging; the visible Write about this flow is declared separately.

A person lets a habit rest during a Metta Return arc, then leaves the arc, and takes the habit up again from the Return surface -- no long-press on a locked tile, no 3-dot menu. The press is asserted on the server rather than on the card: the release row reads re-committed and the habit itself is unlocked again in the account's own habit list, which is the collection read that reconciles auto-reveals, so the pause is shown outranking the program's schedule while it holds and releasing it afterwards. That the row and not merely the habit recorded the re-commit is probed by locking the habit by hand from Habit Settings, which is the only thing that can tell the two halves of the reported flag apart. It runs in the browser lane because the journey is the card: the recovery affordance renders only on a shelf whose arc has ended while a release is outstanding, and the API lane cannot mount a React Native screen at all, so a spec there could only POST the route by hand. Deliberately under-claimed: only the recovery is pressed. Beginning the Return is its own journey (return.begin-a-return-from-the-journal-entry), and the let-go card that releases habits renders only in the session that started the arc, so release-then-leave is arranged over the same live wire -- every step read back, and Orange-stage eligibility asserted false before and true after the tests.e2e.program_anchor rewind, so an arrange that did nothing fails where it happened instead of leaving the press to test an empty shelf. The cross-tenant arm presses the same route from a second account holding an arc of its own: somebody else's habit id reads exactly like a nonexistent one, and the owner's own press afterwards proves that refusal is a refusal rather than a route that moves nothing. Verified to be a live gate: with recommit resolving the active arc again, as it did before the arc-spanning fix, the press 404s and the spec fails.

A person begins a Return from the Journal shelf's offer card and is asked which habits to set down; while they are choosing, the app's own proactive timer renews the same account's token (#3374). Before the fix the let-go card's visibility reset on every credential rotation, because the Return hook mints a new staleness fence per token, so the renewal unmounted the card mid-choice and the active-arc card offered no way back. The covering spec reaches the offer honestly (eligibility via the program anchor, a contraction from a real resonance pass), chooses a habit, then jumps the page clock past the sliding-renewal deadline so the real AuthContext issues POST /auth/refresh against the live server, holding the response only while the clock is set back to the present. It asserts the card and the half-made choice survive the renewal (Release stays live), that the release then leaves with the renewed bearer and exactly the chosen habit id and is recorded on the server, and that Keep them all still closes the moment without a release. Account replacement (A to B, A to B to A) and session teardown still close the card and fence old callbacks; those halves are pinned in Jest (useMettaReturnOwnership.test.tsx, ReturnStackTokenRenewal.test.tsx). #3452 extends that same lineage contract to a held Return-offer decline: proactive renewal and its own 401-refresh-retry land the returned episode once, while a fresh same-owner auth session still refuses the held answer. Reads inside that surviving lineage are ordered independently: an older credential's GET cannot overwrite a newer GET, a completed decline, or a completed start mutation. Frames at 390 and 1280 px, normal and doubled card text, are written to e2e/artifacts/return-letgo-renewal-3374.

A writer's paid Journal work crosses a same-account token renewal and still settles where they asked for it (#3387, #3409, #3411). Each case holds one request at the browser's edge, lets the app's own proactive timer renew the token against the live server, then releases it: the server has revoked the token it carried, so it is refused 401 and the client's refresh-retry resends it with the renewed bearer, exactly once. A note's first letter asked for across the renewal lands instead of spinning forever; a Get resonance press whose wallet read crosses it opens the payer disclosure instead of doing nothing; and a reading refused 402 on its renewed retry opens the refill remedy instead of swallowing the refusal (that 402 body is answered at the edge, since the lane's wallet is full). usePaymentScope fences on the authenticated session lineage (owner, account generation, auth session) rather than the exact JWT, so the same account signing back in after a 401, another account, an A to B to A switch and sign-out still refuse held work; those halves, and the success/failure/402/401-retry outcomes, are pinned through the real AuthProvider and API client in src/features/Journal/__tests__/paymentLineageRenewal.integration.test.tsx. Frames at 390 and 1280 px are written to e2e/artifacts/journal-payment-renewal.

A journal entry whose resonance pass offers the Return is the card a person can begin one from: "Begin the Return" opens a confirmation naming the arc's five weekly foci as the server sent them, confirming opens an arc that lands on week one, and "Not now" persists the same decline the Journal shelf's offer card writes, so declining in the entry is honoured there. It runs in the browser lane because the journey is the card: the offer surfaces only while a resonance pass has just raised the in-memory contraction signal (src/store/useContractionSignalStore.ts) that useMettaReturn reads, and that store is fed by the screen's own pass -- the API lane cannot mount a screen at all, so a spec there could only call the two routes by hand. Both preconditions are arranged honestly: the contraction over the wire, from a habit whose foundation has been quiet past the detection window, and the Orange-stage eligibility by rewinding program_started_at through tests.e2e.program_anchor (no request schema accepts it) and then reading GET /stages, which is what records the entry -- eligibility is asserted false before and true after, so an arrange that did nothing fails rather than silently testing the simple_ease_off card. The double-tap latch is the one arm left to the Jest spec beside the component (src/features/Journal/__tests__/ContractionReflectionNote.test.tsx), which drives it deterministically; a browser cannot dispatch the second press without racing the first request. Verified to be a live gate: with confirmStart no longer calling start(), the spec fails on the arc POST that never leaves the browser. Return declines round-trip the opaque account-bound offer identity observed from the real server (#3299, a bounded child of #3073). The entry posts that exact identity and its observed browser credential. At 390 and 1280 pixels, targeted 200% Return-card text stays within the card and viewport, decline targets retain 44px geometry, and a focused keyboard Enter sets aside the card. Refusing only the real dismissal endpoint with 503 through all three normal transport attempts retains the exact account/episode local pending choice; after the interceptor is removed, returning to the shelf retries that same episode to a real 200, and the following real reload honors its confirmed choice without opening an arc. A held real POST reaches the normal server after the isolated database calendar advances and GET /stages records the later eligible stage; it receives 409, and the next real consumer mount observes the new episode undismissed and offers it through a fresh journal resonance pass. The entry decline unmounts its own hook, so this browser case does not claim an immediate refresh from that removed lifecycle. Real A/B/A/B sign-out and sign-in preserve A's confirmed episode choice while B remains offered its distinct episode. Eligibility is arranged only through the existing isolated program-anchor helper and verified through the real API, while contraction is produced by real habit/journal/resonance handlers. Backend controls cover stale, missing, cross-account, idempotent and commit-boundary progress changes; normal frontend controls cover unknown old global bytes, failed storage, captured identities, A-to-B-to-A late completions, retained callbacks and mounted-consumer 409 refresh. Those delayed-promise controls are not represented as browser-held account-response coverage. Existing server history, eligibility and cadence remain unchanged.

A person whose reflections are still drawn from their last few entries is told so, in the sentence that is true for their own account: the consent decision if they have not made it -- with what saying yes gives, in the same words Settings uses (#3003) -- the import surface if they have and a vault is attached or unknown, or -- since #3017, for an account the server says has nothing attached -- Where your writing lives, under the call to action 'Give your writing a place to live'. The band is declinable in one tap, renders no count, and never blocks resonance. The lane drives the two states and the move between them across the wire on its own account.

A writer can set aside the one-time explanation of where reflections come from without losing the corpus door. A cold reload proves the dismissal persists; the Journal drawer then remains the corpus's sole Journal surface, beside the icon-bearing Photograph a page action, and a fresh undecided account reaches the actual consent screen through a live GET /corpus/voice-readiness decision. The two mounted drawer hosts and the gathering arms -- to the import surface with a vault attached or unknown, and to Where your writing lives with nothing attached (#3017) -- are pinned in the adjacent component suites because the browser starts from only one readiness state. Retrying a failed 'Load older entries' in the same drawer asks again for the missing page and keeps the entries already shown (#2997); pinned in JournalDrawer.test.tsx because the e2e lane cannot force a mid-list failure. The same spec holds the drawer's door and every icon around it to the web's accessibility tree (#3009, #2829): with the console watched from the first page, the anonymous /get-started and /login pages (negative controls), the signed-in Journal shelf, the opened Journal drawer, the feedback composer and a new journal page each carry no React Native-only accessibility prop (accessible, accessibilityElementsHidden, importantForAccessibility) as a DOM attribute; the drawer toggle's svg, the Send feedback icon and the page's close X are aria-hidden="true"; and React logs no non-boolean-attribute or unknown-prop complaint about any of them. The one spelling behind it, decorativeHidden(), and the source guard that holds every file to it are pinned in Jest (a11yHidden.test.ts, decorativeHiddenGuard.test.ts).

At 1280x720 the floating glass timer leaves the visible writing field unobscured. Its idle choice and running rail never shrink the sheet; expanded options remain inside the paper around the desktop rail breakpoint. Finish and Get Resonance remain hit-testable while a session runs and beneath its bounded finished-session note. A 390x640 phone with sixteen server-created habits can scroll to the first and last choices, cancel, and close without covering either page action, then links its final minute-counting habit over the real API and reads the persisted choice back. At 844x390 and 1280x390 with normal and doubled text, and at intermediate 560px height with doubled text, measured natural content makes the whole finished surface scroll: summary, habit offer, Close and compact timer remain usable, and Finish/Get Resonance clear it at the true page bottom. Resizing a sixteen-habit picker through a short viewport preserves its state. Live doubled-text clock glyphs fit the unchanged 44px desktop rail, with no editor overlap and exact paused/resumed countdown verification. Finishing still reaches the server-backed reading view (#3131, #3205).

A person sets a length on the journal's writing timer, writes until it runs out, is offered the session as a habit, and chooses where it sits among the habits they already signed up for — first position by default, with every other habit moving along one stage. The spec drives that write on its own account: it creates the habits the writer already had, then makes the placement the offer makes — one POST for the new habit carrying its stage and its place, one PUT per displaced row carrying theirs — and reads the list back. What only a live server can answer is whether the placement survives: that PUT /habits/{habit_id} keeps sort_order and stage instead of replacing them with the schema defaults, and that GET /habits/ then returns the rows in the order those numbers name, which is what makes the arrangement outlive a cold rehydrate. It also settles the lock: the row is created revealed=false like every other new habit, and the server's own one-shot reconciliation then opens it because Beige is a stage the writer has already reached — the spec pins both halves, and a habit at a stage they have not reached stays locked in the same pass. The offer's own rules (one-tap decline, a decline never re-asked, the stage preview) are pinned by the Jest specs beside WritingSessionOffer, and the offer's reachability from the writing page by JournalEntryScreenTimer.test.tsx; neither can cross the wire. What this spec cannot drive is the half-failure, because no live lane can refuse ONE displacing PUT in the middle of a fan-out: a POST that lands followed by a PUT that does not used to roll back the store alone, leaving a habit on the server the writer never confirmed under copy saying their habits were as they were. That branch is pinned beside habitManager instead (habitManager.test.ts: the created row is taken back off by the id its own POST returned; the branch where that DELETE is itself refused says the habit was saved out of place rather than reassuring; and a confirming re-fetch that fails after every write landed is not reported as a failed write).

A person finishes a timed writing session and is offered — beside the habit offer, under the same single decline — to keep it as the Journaling practice at Green. The offer describes what keeping it would do BEFORE it writes anything, because two things it would do are invisible from the journal page: Green may already hold a practice the writer chose (the server resolves a second open selection by closing the first, so a bare write evicts it silently), and Green may not be open to them yet (the selection is allowed as forward planning, but the just-finished session cannot be logged against it). This spec drives the server half on its own account, from a fresh signup standing at Beige — the harder half. It reads the seeded catalogue at stage 6 and pins that Journaling is there, approved, count_up, and twenty minutes; selects it at Green from Beige and pins that the server ACCEPTS the forward-planned pick, which is what makes the flow possible at all given that a mismatched stage_number is refused; pins that POST /practice-sessions/ against it is 403 stage_locked, which is why the client declines to send one and says so instead; reads the selection back by the effective_name the offer shows; and then puts another practice at Green and pins that the first row is CLOSED rather than the write refused — the silent eviction the offer names before the tap. The offer's own rules (one-tap decline, a decline never re-asked, the sentence shown before the write, no session claimed that was not logged) are pinned by the Jest specs beside WritingSessionOffer and SaveAsPracticeStep; none of them can cross the wire.

A writing timer logs the amount it measured to the linked open server habit: elapsed rounded minutes (at least one, including an early stop), or one full session for a sessions habit. A second session adds its own amount. The real Chromium witness chooses an existing habit through the offer and confirms its server link, checks POST /goal_completions/ carries the measured completed_units and via_timer:true, verifies a distinct operation identity for each session, and reads the accumulated server totals after repeated sessions, early stop and reload. A sessions habit counts a complete session and ignores an early stop. A committing first request whose response is deliberately replaced by a 503 proves the generic retry keeps its Idempotency-Key and adds the measured minutes once. Confirmed amount notices appear beneath the session summary; unconfirmed logs claim no success. Deleting the habit clears the server link. The same witness creates an immediately open Journaling habit with atomic 10/20/45 minute goals on an account that already has ten habits, at phone/desktop sizes with enlarged text, then logs ten minutes and reloads. Settings uses the shared picker to convert an unsupported existing unit to sessions, confirms every goal before linking, and retains the link on reload. #3452 pins the two remaining auth boundaries in Jest: a held picker goal-save and a held linked-habit check-off both survive proactive renewal and their own single 401-refresh-retry, but same-owner reauth, sign-out, account switch and A-to-B-to-A refuse the held completion. Unit tests also pin partial-write and delayed-owner refusal; these are scenarios of this one timer-to-habit journey rather than additional coverage counts.

A writer whose writing timer has no habit linked finishes a full-length session and the note it leaves points to Settings, where one can be chosen (#3006). On an ordinary page the keep-this offer has the first note to itself -- one invitation per note -- so declining it adds nothing to that note; the next finished session, with the offer answered and GET /ui-flags still unlinked, carries the link-a-habit note with two actions, Go to Settings and Don't show again.
